JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What is JavaScript primarily designed for in web development?
questions.b: Adding dynamic interactivity, behavior, and logic to web pages on the client side
questions.explanation: JavaScript is the standard programming language of the web that adds client-side dynamic interactivity and behavior to HTML pages.

questions.question: Which HTML tag is used to embed or reference client-side JavaScript code?
questions.b: <script>
questions.explanation: The <script> element contains client-side JavaScript code or points to an external script file via src.

questions.question: Which method is commonly used to write formatted diagnostic messages into the browser's Developer Console?
questions.b: console.log()
questions.explanation: console.log() writes output data and objects directly to the browser's developer debugging console.

questions.question: Which method displays a modal alert dialog box with a message and an OK button to the user?
questions.b: alert()
questions.explanation: window.alert() displays a blocking modal dialog containing a message and an OK button.

questions.question: Which property is used to access or modify the HTML content inside a DOM element directly in JavaScript?
questions.b: element.innerHTML
questions.explanation: element.innerHTML gets or sets the HTML markup contained within the element.

questions.question: Which property is preferred over innerHTML when inserting plain text to avoid Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities?
questions.b: textContent
questions.explanation: textContent safely sets or returns text without parsing HTML tags, preventing XSS injection risks.

questions.question: What happens if document.write() is executed after the HTML document has fully loaded?
questions.a: It writes at the bottom of the page
questions.b: It completely erases and overwrites the entire existing HTML document
questions.c: It opens a new browser window
questions.d: It logs an error in console without changing the page
questions.explanation: Calling document.write() after page load completely blows away the existing document and overwrites it.

questions.question: Which method opens a modal prompt dialog that allows the user to enter text input?
questions.b: window.prompt()
questions.explanation: prompt(message, default) opens a modal dialog requesting string input from the user (returns null if cancelled).

questions.question: Which method displays a modal confirmation box with OK and Cancel buttons, returning true or false?
questions.b: window.decision()
questions.explanation: confirm() displays a modal dialog with OK (returns true) and Cancel (returns false).

questions.question: How do you write a single-line comment in JavaScript?
questions.b: // Single line comment
questions.explanation: // starts a single-line comment in JavaScript syntax.

questions.question: How do you write a multi-line comment in JavaScript?
questions.b: /* Multi-line comment */
questions.explanation: /* ... */ delimits multi-line block comments in JavaScript.

questions.question: What is the standard file extension used for external JavaScript files?
questions.b: .js
questions.explanation: Standard JavaScript source files use the '.js' file extension.

questions.question: Is JavaScript a case-sensitive programming language?
questions.b: Yes, 'myVariable' and 'myvariable' are two completely separate identifiers
questions.d: Only when running on Linux servers
questions.explanation: JavaScript is strictly case-sensitive for all identifiers, keywords, variables, and function names.

questions.question: What is camelCase naming convention commonly used for in JavaScript?
questions.b: Starting with a lowercase letter and capitalizing each subsequent concatenated word (e.g., firstName, calculateTotalAmount)
questions.explanation: lowerCamelCase (e.g. getElementById) is standard convention for JS variables and function names.

questions.question: What is Automatic Semicolon Insertion (ASI) in JavaScript?
questions.a: A feature in VS Code that formats files on save
questions.b: A JavaScript parser mechanism that automatically inserts semicolons at certain line breaks to complete statements
questions.explanation: ASI allows omitting trailing semicolons in many cases by automatically inferring statement boundaries during parsing.

questions.question: What is the ECMAScript standard (ES)?
questions.b: The official standardized specification upon which JavaScript implementations (V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore) are based
questions.explanation: ECMAScript (ECMA-262) is the official specification standardized by TC39 defining the JavaScript language.

questions.question: What major version of ECMAScript released in 2015 introduced let, const, arrow functions, classes, and promises?
questions.b: ES6 (ECMAScript 2015)
questions.explanation: ES6 (ES2015) was a landmark release modernizing JavaScript with classes, modules, promises, let/const, and arrow functions.

questions.question: What does the 'use strict'; directive do when placed at the beginning of a script or function?
questions.a: Forces the browser to compile code into C++
questions.b: Enables Strict Mode, catching silent bugs, throwing errors on undeclared globals, and preventing unsafe actions
questions.explanation: 'use strict' enforces strict mode, preventing undeclared global variables, eliminating 'this' coercion, and reserving future keywords.

questions.question: What happens if you assign a value to an undeclared variable (e.g., x = 10;) in Strict Mode?
questions.a: It automatically declares a global variable
questions.b: It throws a ReferenceError: x is not defined
questions.c: It creates a local variable in the nearest function
questions.d: It converts x to a string
questions.explanation: In strict mode, assigning to an undeclared variable throws a ReferenceError instead of silently creating a window global.

questions.question: Which JavaScript console method formats output as an interactive tabular grid?
questions.b: console.table()
questions.explanation: console.table() renders arrays and objects as clean tabular data in developer tools.

questions.question: Which console methods are used to measure the exact execution time of a code block?
questions.b: console.time() and console.timeEnd()
questions.explanation: console.time('label') starts a timer and console.timeEnd('label') outputs elapsed milliseconds.

questions.question: Which console method outputs an interactive hierarchical tree view of an object's properties?
questions.b: console.dir()
questions.explanation: console.dir() lists all properties of a specified JavaScript object in an interactive collapsible tree.

questions.question: Which console method prints a stack trace showing how the code reached the current execution point?
questions.b: console.trace()
questions.explanation: console.trace() outputs a complete call stack trace to the debugging console.

questions.question: Which keyword can be placed in JavaScript code to programmatically trigger a breakpoint in the browser debugger?
questions.b: debugger;
questions.explanation: The 'debugger;' statement invokes any available debugging functionality (like pausing in Chrome DevTools).

questions.question: What is the global object in a standard web browser environment?
questions.b: window
questions.explanation: In web browsers, the 'window' object represents the top-level global execution context and global scope.

questions.question: What global identifier introduced in ES2020 provides a standardized reference to the global object across all JS environments (browsers, Node.js, Web Workers)?
questions.b: globalThis
questions.explanation: 'globalThis' provides a unified, cross-platform standard property to access the global object.

questions.question: Where in an HTML document is it generally recommended to place heavy external script tags without async/defer to avoid blocking initial DOM rendering?
questions.b: Just before the closing </body> tag
questions.explanation: Placing traditional synchronous script tags before </body> ensures HTML content parses and renders before scripts block.

questions.question: What is a JavaScript engine?
questions.b: A program or virtual machine (like Google V8, Mozilla SpiderMonkey) that executes and compiles JavaScript code to machine instructions
questions.explanation: A JavaScript engine parses, JIT-compiles, and executes JavaScript code into native machine code.

questions.question: What is Just-In-Time (JIT) Compilation in modern JavaScript engines?
questions.a: Compiling code in the cloud before uploading
questions.b: Compiling JavaScript bytecode into optimized native machine code dynamically during runtime for high performance
questions.explanation: Modern JS engines use JIT compilation to profile runtime execution and dynamically optimize hot code paths into machine instructions.

questions.question: What is a polyfill in JavaScript?
questions.b: A piece of code (or plugin) used to provide modern standard functionality on older browsers that lack native support
questions.c: A tool that minifies CSS styles
questions.explanation: A polyfill replicates modern standard API methods (like Promise or Array.prototype.includes) for legacy browser engines.

questions.question: Which keyword was traditionally used to declare variables in JavaScript prior to ES6?
questions.b: var
questions.explanation: 'var' was the original variable declaration keyword in JavaScript prior to ES6 (2015).

questions.question: What type of scope do variables declared with 'var' have?
questions.b: Function scope (or global scope if declared outside any function)
questions.explanation: 'var' variables are scoped to the nearest enclosing function context, completely ignoring '{ ... }' code blocks like if/for.

questions.question: What type of scope do variables declared with 'let' and 'const' have?
questions.b: Block scope (limited to the enclosing curly braces { })
questions.explanation: 'let' and 'const' are strictly block-scoped, existing only within the enclosing pair of braces { }.

questions.question: Can a variable declared with 'const' be reassigned to a new value after initialization?
questions.b: No, attempting to reassign a const variable throws a TypeError: Assignment to constant variable
questions.d: Only if reassigned to the same data type
questions.explanation: 'const' creates an immutable variable binding that cannot be reassigned; doing so throws a TypeError.

questions.question: Can you declare a 'const' variable without providing an initial value (e.g. const x;)?
questions.b: No, const declarations must be initialized with a value upon declaration (throws SyntaxError: Missing initializer)
questions.d: Only if initialized within the next 3 lines
questions.explanation: A 'const' declaration requires an immediate initializer expression; omitting it produces a SyntaxError.

questions.question: If an array or object is declared with 'const', can its internal properties or elements be modified/mutated?
questions.a: No, the object and all its properties become completely frozen and read-only
questions.b: Yes, the variable binding is immutable, but the underlying object/array itself remains fully mutable
questions.explanation: 'const' prevents reassigning the variable identifier to a new memory reference, but does not freeze object properties or array items.

questions.question: What JavaScript method makes an object completely immutable, preventing adding, deleting, or modifying existing properties?
questions.b: Object.freeze()
questions.explanation: Object.freeze(obj) makes an object shallowly immutable so existing properties cannot be changed or removed.

questions.question: What is 'Hoisting' in JavaScript?
questions.a: Lifting DOM elements to the top layer
questions.b: The engine's behavior of allocating memory for variable and function declarations before code execution begins
questions.explanation: Hoisting is the behavior where variable and function declarations are registered in memory during the compilation phase before execution.

questions.question: What is the value of 'a' when accessed before its declaration: 'console.log(a); var a = 10;'?
questions.b: undefined
questions.explanation: Variables declared with 'var' are hoisted and initialized with 'undefined' prior to execution.

questions.question: What happens when accessing a 'let' or 'const' variable before its declaration line in source code?
questions.b: Throws a ReferenceError (due to the Temporal Dead Zone)
questions.explanation: Accessing a 'let' or 'const' variable before its declaration throws a ReferenceError because the variable is in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ).

questions.question: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)?
questions.a: A timeout period for aborted network requests
questions.b: The region of code from the start of the enclosing block until the variable's declaration is reached, where accessing let/const variables throws ReferenceError
questions.c: The time spent during garbage collection
questions.d: A deprecation window for obsolete APIs
questions.explanation: The TDZ is the zone within a block before a let/const variable is declared, during which any read/write access throws a ReferenceError.

questions.question: Can a variable declared with 'let' or 'const' be redeclared within the same scope block?
questions.a: Yes, the second declaration silently overwrites the first
questions.b: No, attempting to redeclare it in the same scope produces a SyntaxError: Identifier has already been declared
questions.explanation: Unlike 'var', redeclaring an identifier with 'let' or 'const' in the same scope is illegal and causes a SyntaxError.

questions.question: Can a variable declared with 'var' be redeclared multiple times in the same scope?
questions.b: Yes, 'var' allows redundant redeclarations without error in the same scope
questions.explanation: Redeclaring a 'var' variable in the same scope is permitted by JavaScript and simply acts as an assignment if initialized.

questions.question: What does the following code output: { var x = 2; } console.log(x); ?
questions.explanation: 'var' is not block-scoped, so x leaks out of the plain '{ ... }' block into the outer scope.

questions.question: What does the following code output: { let x = 2; } console.log(x); ?
questions.b: ReferenceError: x is not defined
questions.explanation: 'let' is block-scoped, so 'x' exists only inside the curly braces and is not accessible outside.

questions.question: Does declaring a global variable with 'var' in a browser environment attach it as a property of the 'window' object?
questions.b: Yes, 'var myGlobal = 5;' creates 'window.myGlobal = 5'
questions.explanation: Top-level 'var' declarations attach properties to the global window object in browsers.

questions.question: Does declaring a global variable with 'let' or 'const' attach it as a property of the 'window' object?
questions.b: No, top-level let and const create global lexical bindings without creating properties on the window object
questions.d: Only if initialized with an object
questions.explanation: Global let and const declarations are stored in the global declarative environment record, not as window properties.

questions.question: What is 'Variable Shadowing' in JavaScript?
questions.a: Deleting variables when they go out of scope
questions.b: Declaring a variable in an inner scope with the same name as a variable in an outer scope, temporarily masking the outer variable
questions.d: Making variables invisible to debugger tools
questions.explanation: Shadowing occurs when an inner block identifier hides an outer identifier of identical name within the inner block.

questions.question: What is the Scope Chain in JavaScript execution context?
questions.a: A linked list of network connections
questions.b: The hierarchical resolution mechanism where the engine looks up an identifier in the local scope, then parent scopes, up to the global scope
questions.d: A sequence of CSS selector rules
questions.explanation: The scope chain allows inner execution contexts to search outwards through outer parent scopes to resolve variable names.

questions.question: What is Lexical Scope (Static Scope) in JavaScript?
questions.a: Scope determined at runtime by who calls the function
questions.b: Scope determined at author/compile time by the physical location where functions and variables are written in the source code
questions.c: Scope stored in external JSON files
questions.d: Scope limited strictly to 10 lines of code
questions.explanation: Lexical scoping means variable access is dictated by the author's physical placement of code blocks, not call stack history.

questions.question: Which of the following is an invalid identifier name in JavaScript?
questions.b: $price
questions.explanation: JavaScript identifiers cannot start with a numeric digit (0-9). They must start with a letter, $, or _.

questions.question: Can JavaScript reserved keywords (like 'if', 'while', 'class', 'function') be used as variable names?
questions.b: No, reserved keywords cannot be used as variable identifiers (causes SyntaxError)
questions.explanation: Reserved words are preserved for language syntax and cannot be declared as variable or function identifiers.

questions.question: What is the default value of a declared variable that has not been initialized with any value (e.g. let score;)?
questions.b: undefined
questions.explanation: Variables declared without an explicit initial value automatically hold the primitive value 'undefined'.

questions.question: What does the following classic loop print: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100); } ?
questions.explanation: Because 'var' is function-scoped, all timeouts share the single mutated variable 'i', which reaches 3 when the loop finishes.

questions.question: What does the loop print when using 'let': for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100); } ?
questions.explanation: 'let' creates a brand-new lexical binding for 'i' for every single iteration of the loop, preserving 0, 1, and 2 for each closure.

questions.question: What happens if you declare a variable without any keyword (e.g. x = 5;) inside a function in non-strict mode?
questions.a: It is destroyed when the function returns
questions.b: It accidentally creates an implicit global variable on the window object
questions.c: It throws a fatal syntax error
questions.explanation: In sloppy (non-strict) mode, assigning to an undeclared identifier creates an implicit global variable on the global object.

questions.question: What is a Closure in JavaScript?
questions.a: A method that closes the browser window
questions.b: The combination of a function bundled together with references to its surrounding lexical environment (retaining access to outer variables even after the outer function has returned)
questions.explanation: A closure gives a function access to its outer lexical scope even when invoked outside that scope.

questions.question: What is an Immediately Invoked Function Expression (IIFE)?
questions.a: A function that executes only when the user clicks
questions.b: A JavaScript function that runs as soon as it is defined, commonly used to create private local scopes prior to ES6 let/const
questions.explanation: An IIFE: (function() { ... })(); executes immediately, isolating variables to prevent polluting the global namespace.

questions.question: What is the recommended modern best practice for declaring variables in JavaScript?
questions.b: Use 'const' by default; use 'let' only when you know the variable's value must be reassigned; avoid 'var'
questions.c: Always omit keywords to save bytes
questions.d: Use let for all variables and never use const
questions.explanation: Modern JavaScript best practice dictates using 'const' by default to signal immutability and 'let' only when reassignment is needed.

questions.question: Can multiple variables be declared in a single statement separated by commas (e.g. let a = 1, b = 2, c = 3;)?
questions.a: No, each variable requires its own let keyword on separate lines
questions.b: Yes, multiple variables can be declared and initialized in a single comma-separated statement
questions.explanation: Comma-separated variable declarations (let x = 1, y = 2;) are valid syntax in JavaScript.

questions.question: How many primitive data types are defined in modern ECMAScript (ES2020+)?
questions.b: 7 (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, null)
questions.explanation: JavaScript has 7 primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, and null (plus the non-primitive 'object').

questions.question: What is returned by 'typeof 42'?
questions.b: "number"
questions.explanation: All standard numeric values (integers and floating-point) belong to the primitive type 'number'.

questions.question: What is returned by 'typeof "Hello"'?
questions.b: "string"
questions.explanation: Text sequences are primitive strings, returning 'string' from typeof.

questions.question: What is returned by 'typeof true'?
questions.b: "boolean"
questions.explanation: Boolean literals true and false return 'boolean' from the typeof operator.

questions.question: What is returned by 'typeof undefined'?
questions.b: "undefined"
questions.explanation: The typeof operator returns 'undefined' for unassigned variables or the undefined literal.

questions.question: What is returned by 'typeof null' in JavaScript?
questions.b: "object" (a famous historical bug in JS since its initial 1995 implementation)
questions.explanation: typeof null returns 'object' due to a legacy 1995 implementation detail where null had a 000 type tag.

questions.question: What is returned by 'typeof [1, 2, 3]'?
questions.b: "object"
questions.explanation: Arrays in JavaScript are specialized objects, so typeof returns 'object'. Use Array.isArray() to check for arrays.

questions.question: What is returned by 'typeof function() {}'?
questions.b: "function"
questions.explanation: Although functions are callable objects, typeof has a special case that returns 'function'.

questions.question: What format does JavaScript use to represent all standard 'number' values internally?
questions.b: IEEE 754 double-precision 64-bit binary floating-point format
questions.explanation: Standard JS numbers are IEEE 754 64-bit floating-point numbers (doubles).

questions.question: Why does '0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3' evaluate to false in JavaScript?
questions.a: JavaScript converts numbers to strings before adding
questions.b: Because 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be represented with exact precision in binary floating-point (evaluating to 0.30000000000000004)
questions.c: Strict equality does not work on decimal numbers
questions.d: 0.1 is rounded to 0 by the engine
questions.explanation: Binary floating-point arithmetic introduces tiny rounding discrepancies (0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004).

questions.question: What primitive type introduced in ES2020 allows working with integers of arbitrary size larger than 2^53 - 1?
questions.b: BigInt
questions.explanation: BigInt (created by appending 'n' to an integer, e.g., 9007199254740995n) supports arbitrarily large integers.

questions.question: What is the value of 'Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER' in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is (2^53 - 1) = 9007199254740991, the highest integer representable without loss of precision.

questions.question: What is 'NaN' in JavaScript?
questions.b: Not-a-Number (a special numeric value representing the result of an invalid mathematical computation, like 0 / 0 or Math.sqrt(-1))
questions.explanation: NaN stands for Not-a-Number, indicating an uncomputable or invalid numeric result.

questions.question: What is the return value of 'typeof NaN'?
questions.b: "number"
questions.explanation: Ironical as it sounds, NaN is of type 'number' in JavaScript.

questions.question: What does 'NaN === NaN' evaluate to in JavaScript?
questions.b: false (NaN is the only value in JavaScript that is not equal to itself)
questions.explanation: Per IEEE 754 standards, NaN compares unequal to all values, including itself (NaN === NaN is false). Use Number.isNaN().

questions.question: What is the difference between global 'isNaN(val)' and 'Number.isNaN(val)'?
questions.b: Global isNaN() coerces values to numbers first (e.g. isNaN('hello') is true); Number.isNaN() strictly checks if the value is of type number and exactly NaN
questions.d: Global isNaN() is deprecated and throws errors
questions.explanation: Number.isNaN() is robust because it does not coerce non-numeric strings to NaN before checking.

questions.question: What does dividing a positive number by zero (e.g., 5 / 0) produce in JavaScript?
questions.b: Infinity
questions.explanation: In JavaScript, dividing a non-zero positive number by 0 yields 'Infinity' (or '-Infinity' for negative numbers).

questions.question: What is the result of 'Math.round(4.5)' vs 'Math.round(4.4)'?
questions.b: 4 and 4
questions.explanation: Math.round() rounds to the nearest integer, rounding .5 upwards (4.5 becomes 5; 4.4 becomes 4).

questions.question: What does 'Math.ceil(4.1)' evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Math.ceil() always rounds a number UPWARDS to the next largest integer (4.1 becomes 5).

questions.question: What does 'Math.floor(4.9)' evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Math.floor() rounds a number DOWNWARDS to the next smallest integer (4.9 becomes 4).

questions.question: What does 'Math.trunc(4.9)' do in ES6?
questions.b: Returns the integer part of a number by simply removing any fractional digits (4.9 becomes 4; -4.9 becomes -4)
questions.explanation: Math.trunc() chops off the decimal part without rounding up or down.

questions.question: What does 'Math.random()' return in JavaScript?
questions.b: A floating-point pseudo-random number in the range [0, 1) (inclusive of 0, but strictly less than 1)
questions.explanation: Math.random() generates a pseudo-random floating-point number from 0 (inclusive) up to but not including 1.

questions.question: How do you generate a random integer between 1 and 10 (inclusive)?
questions.b: Math.floor(Math.random() * 10) + 1
questions.explanation: Math.floor(Math.random() * 10) gives 0-9; adding 1 yields a uniform integer range from 1 to 10.

questions.question: What does 'Math.max(10, 20, 5, 40, 15)' return?
questions.explanation: Math.max() returns the largest of the zero or more numbers given as input arguments.

questions.question: What does 'Math.min(10, 20, 5, 40, 15)' return?
questions.explanation: Math.min() returns the smallest number among the provided parameters.

questions.question: What does 'Math.abs(-25)' return?
questions.explanation: Math.abs() returns the absolute (non-negative) value of a number.

questions.question: What method formats a number using fixed-point notation with a specified number of decimal digits (e.g. (3.14159).toFixed(2))?
questions.b: toFixed()
questions.explanation: num.toFixed(2) formats a number to 2 decimal places and returns the result as a string (e.g. '3.14').

questions.question: What does 'parseInt("42px")' return in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: parseInt() parses leading numeric characters from a string until hitting a non-digit, returning 42.

questions.question: What does 'Number("42px")' return in JavaScript?
questions.b: NaN
questions.explanation: The Number() type constructor performs strict conversion and returns NaN if any non-numeric character is present.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'Symbol' primitive type introduced in ES6?
questions.b: Creating completely unique, immutable identifiers often used as collision-free private object property keys
questions.explanation: Symbol() creates a unique, anonymous token guaranteed never to clash with any other property key.

questions.question: What is the strict equality operator in JavaScript that checks both value AND data type without coercion?
questions.explanation: The '===' (strict equality) operator checks that both operands have the identical value and type without performing type coercion.

questions.question: What does '5 == "5"' evaluate to in JavaScript?
questions.b: true
questions.explanation: The loose equality operator '==' converts the string "5" to number 5 before comparison, evaluating to true.

questions.question: What does '5 === "5"' evaluate to in JavaScript?
questions.b: false
questions.explanation: The strict equality operator '===' compares types first (number vs string) and evaluates immediately to false.

questions.question: What is the strict inequality operator in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: '!==' tests inequality with strict type and value checking.

questions.question: What does the exponentiation operator '**' perform (e.g. 2 ** 3)?
questions.b: Raises the base to the power of the exponent (2^3 = 8, equivalent to Math.pow(2, 3))
questions.explanation: The '**' operator (added in ES2016) calculates base raised to an exponent.

questions.question: What is the result of '10 % 3' in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: The remainder (modulus) operator '%' yields the integer remainder of 10 divided by 3, which is 1.

questions.question: What is the difference between postfix increment 'x++' and prefix increment '++x'?
questions.a: Prefix increments by 2; postfix increments by 1
questions.b: '++x' increments x and evaluates to the new value; 'x++' evaluates to the current value of x before incrementing
questions.c: Postfix works only on floating points
questions.d: There is no difference in any context
questions.explanation: Prefix '++x' increments first then returns the updated value; postfix 'x++' returns the original value before incrementing.

questions.question: What is the result of: let x = 5; let y = x++; console.log(y, x); ?
questions.explanation: y receives the original value 5 before x increments to 6.

questions.question: What does the unary plus operator '+' do when applied to a string (e.g. +"42")?
questions.b: Attempts to convert its operand into a number (equivalent to Number("42"))
questions.c: Checks if the number is positive
questions.explanation: Unary plus (+operand) is a fast idiom to convert strings or booleans into numbers.

questions.question: What does the nullish coalescing operator '??' do in JavaScript (ES2020)?
questions.a: Returns false if both operands are null
questions.b: Returns its right-hand operand when its left-hand operand is null or undefined; otherwise returns the left-hand operand
questions.d: Compares if two variables are undefined
questions.explanation: The '??' operator returns the right-side fallback ONLY if the left side is null or undefined (unlike ||, which falls back on 0 or "").

questions.question: What is the critical difference between '0 || 10' and '0 ?? 10'?
questions.a: '0 || 10' evaluates to 10 (since 0 is falsy); '0 ?? 10' evaluates to 0 (since 0 is not null or undefined)
questions.b: Both evaluate to 10
questions.explanation: Logical OR (||) treats 0 as falsy and returns 10, whereas nullish coalescing (??) preserves 0 because it is defined.

questions.question: What does the Optional Chaining operator '?.' do (e.g. user?.profile?.avatar)?
questions.a: Creates a backup copy of user
questions.b: Safely reads deep nested properties without throwing a TypeError if an intermediate reference is null or undefined (returning undefined instead)
questions.d: Converts null to empty objects automatically
questions.explanation: Optional chaining ('?.') short-circuits to undefined if the reference before '?.' is nullish, preventing 'Cannot read property of undefined' crashes.

questions.question: What does the logical AND assignment operator 'x &&= y;' do in ES2021?
questions.a: Assigns y to x only if x is truthy (x && (x = y))
questions.b: Performs bitwise AND and assigns
questions.d: Throws an error if x is false
questions.explanation: 'x &&= y' assigns y to x only when x evaluates to a truthy value.

questions.question: What does the logical OR assignment operator 'x ||= y;' do in ES2021?
questions.a: Assigns y to x only if x is falsy (x || (x = y))
questions.b: Assigns y to x only if x is truthy
questions.explanation: 'x ||= y' assigns y to x only when x evaluates to a falsy value (used for setting default values).

questions.question: What does the nullish coalescing assignment operator 'x ??= y;' do in ES2021?
questions.a: Assigns y to x only if x is null or undefined (x ?? (x = y))
questions.b: Assigns y to x only if x is 0
questions.explanation: 'x ??= y' assigns y to x only if x is currently null or undefined.

questions.question: What does the 'typeof' operator do?
questions.b: Returns a string indicating the data type of the unevaluated operand
questions.c: Casts a variable to a new type
questions.d: Checks if an object inherits from a class
questions.explanation: typeof returns a string stating the operand's type (e.g., 'number', 'string', 'boolean').

questions.question: What does the 'instanceof' operator check?
questions.a: Checks if a string matches a regular expression
questions.b: Tests whether the prototype property of a constructor appears anywhere within the prototype chain of an object
questions.c: Checks if two numbers are equal
questions.d: Checks if an object is frozen
questions.explanation: object instanceof Constructor verifies if Constructor.prototype exists in object's prototype hierarchy.

questions.question: What does the 'in' operator check (e.g. 'name' in person)?
questions.a: Checks if an item exists inside an array value
questions.b: Returns true if the specified property exists in the object or its prototype chain
questions.explanation: The 'in' operator verifies whether a specified property key exists in an object or anywhere along its prototype chain.

questions.question: What does the 'delete' operator do (e.g. delete user.age;)?
questions.b: Removes a property from an object
questions.c: Deletes a local variable declared with let
questions.d: Clears an entire array to 0 length
questions.explanation: 'delete obj.prop' removes the specified property from the object.

questions.question: What does the 'void' operator do (e.g. void 0)?
questions.b: Evaluates the given expression and returns the primitive value 'undefined'
questions.explanation: The void operator evaluates an expression and unconditionally yields 'undefined' (e.g. void 0).

questions.question: What does the bitwise NOT operator '~' do in JavaScript?
questions.a: Inverts all bits of a 32-bit integer operand (equivalent to -(x + 1))
questions.b: Logical NOT
questions.explanation: Bitwise NOT '~' inverts the 32-bit representation of the operand (e.g., ~5 === -6).

questions.question: What does the zero-fill right shift operator '>>>' do?
questions.a: Shifts bits right and shifts in zeros from the left, producing an unsigned 32-bit integer
questions.b: Shifts bits right while preserving the sign bit
questions.explanation: '>>>' shifts bits right, filling vacant left positions with zeros to always yield an unsigned 32-bit integer.

questions.question: What does the expression '"10" + 5' evaluate to in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: When '+' is used with a string operand, JavaScript performs string concatenation, yielding "105".

questions.question: What does the expression '"10" - 5' evaluate to in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: The subtraction operator '-' has no string concatenation meaning, so it coerces "10" to number 10, resulting in 5.

questions.question: What does 'true + true' evaluate to in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: When arithmetic addition is applied to booleans, 'true' coerces to integer 1, evaluating 1 + 1 = 2.

questions.question: What does '[] + []' evaluate to in JavaScript?
questions.b: "" (empty string)
questions.explanation: Adding two empty arrays invokes .toString() on both, concatenating "" + "" = "".

questions.question: What does '[] + {}' evaluate to in standard JavaScript expressions?
questions.b: "[object Object]"
questions.explanation: [] converts to "" and {} converts to "[object Object]", concatenating to "[object Object]".

questions.question: What is the Ternary (Conditional) Operator syntax in JavaScript?
questions.b: if (condition) -> expr1 else -> expr2
questions.explanation: The ternary operator 'condition ? expr1 : expr2' evaluates condition and returns expr1 if truthy, otherwise expr2.

questions.question: Which operator has higher precedence: Multiplication '*' or Addition '+'?
questions.b: Multiplication (*)
questions.d: Depends on whether strict mode is enabled
questions.explanation: Multiplication has higher operator precedence than addition (e.g. 2 + 3 * 4 = 14).

questions.question: What is the associativity of the Assignment '=' and Exponentiation '**' operators?
questions.b: Right-to-left
questions.explanation: Assignment and exponentiation are right-associative (e.g. a = b = c evaluates as a = (b = c); 2 ** 3 ** 2 evaluates as 2 ** 9 = 512).

questions.question: Which property returns the total number of characters (code units) in a string?
questions.b: str.length
questions.explanation: 'str.length' is a property that returns the character length of the string.

questions.question: Which character is used to delimit modern ES6 Template Literals (Template Strings)?
questions.b: Backticks (` `)
questions.explanation: Template literals are enclosed by backtick characters (` `).

questions.question: How do you embed expressions or variables inside a template literal string (String Interpolation)?
questions.b: ${expression}
questions.explanation: ${expression} inside backticks evaluates the JavaScript expression and inserts its string value.

questions.question: Can template literals natively span multiple lines without escape characters like '\n'?
questions.a: No, line breaks cause a SyntaxError
questions.b: Yes, template literals preserve multiline newlines and formatting naturally
questions.explanation: Template literals preserve real newline characters and whitespace naturally across multiple lines.

questions.question: Which method converts all characters in a string to uppercase?
questions.b: str.toUpperCase()
questions.explanation: str.toUpperCase() returns a new string converted to uppercase letters.

questions.question: Which method converts all characters in a string to lowercase?
questions.b: str.toSmall()
questions.explanation: str.toLowerCase() returns a new string with all characters converted to lowercase.

questions.question: Which method removes whitespace characters from BOTH the beginning and the end of a string?
questions.b: str.trim()
questions.explanation: str.trim() strips leading and trailing whitespace, tabs, and newlines from a string.

questions.question: Which methods remove whitespace specifically from ONLY the start or ONLY the end of a string in ES2019?
questions.b: stripFront() / stripBack()
questions.explanation: trimStart() and trimEnd() (and aliases trimLeft/trimRight) remove whitespace from the respective ends.

questions.question: Which method returns the index of the FIRST occurrence of a substring, or -1 if not found?
questions.b: str.indexOf()
questions.explanation: str.indexOf(searchValue) returns the 0-based index of the first match, or -1 if absent.

questions.question: Which method returns the index of the LAST occurrence of a substring in a string?
questions.b: str.findLast()
questions.explanation: str.lastIndexOf(searchValue) searches backwards from the end of the string.

questions.question: Which ES6 boolean method checks whether a string contains a specified substring anywhere within it?
questions.b: str.includes()
questions.explanation: str.includes(searchString) returns true if the search string is found anywhere within str.

questions.question: Which method checks if a string begins with specified characters?
questions.b: str.beginsWith()
questions.explanation: str.startsWith(searchString) returns true if the string starts with searchString.

questions.question: Which method checks if a string ends with specified characters?
questions.b: str.terminatesWith()
questions.explanation: str.endsWith(searchString) returns true if the string ends with searchString.

questions.question: Which method extracts a section of a string and returns it as a new string without modifying the original (e.g. str.slice(start, end))?
questions.b: str.slice()
questions.explanation: str.slice(startIndex, endIndex) extracts a portion of a string (supports negative indices).

questions.question: What does 'str.slice(-3)' do on string 'JavaScript'?
questions.b: Extracts the last 3 characters ('ipt')
questions.explanation: A negative index in .slice() counts backwards from the end of the string (extracting 'ipt').

questions.question: What does the method 'str.replace(searchValue, newValue)' do when passed a plain string as searchValue?
questions.a: Replaces ALL occurrences in the entire string
questions.b: Replaces ONLY the very FIRST occurrence of the searchValue
questions.explanation: Passing a plain string to str.replace() replaces ONLY the first matching instance.

questions.question: Which method introduced in ES2021 replaces ALL occurrences of a string without requiring a global regex /g flag?
questions.b: str.replaceEvery()
questions.explanation: str.replaceAll('target', 'newVal') replaces all matching occurrences in the string.

questions.question: Which method splits a string into an array of substrings based on a specified separator string?
questions.b: str.split()
questions.explanation: str.split(separator) breaks a string into an array of substrings.

questions.question: What does '"hello".split("")' return?
questions.explanation: Splitting by an empty string ("") breaks the string into an array of individual characters.

questions.question: Which method returns the character at a specified index in a string (e.g. str.charAt(0))?
questions.b: str.charAt()
questions.explanation: str.charAt(index) returns the character at the specified 0-based index.

questions.question: Which ES2022 method allows indexing strings with negative numbers (e.g. str.at(-1) for the last character)?
questions.b: str.at()
questions.explanation: str.at(index) supports negative relative indexing, where str.at(-1) retrieves the last character.

questions.question: Which method returns the Unicode UTF-16 integer code point at a specified index in a string?
questions.b: str.charCodeAt()
questions.explanation: str.charCodeAt(index) returns an integer between 0 and 65535 representing the UTF-16 unit.

questions.question: Which String static method creates a string from a sequence of UTF-16 character codes?
questions.b: String.toChars()
questions.explanation: String.fromCharCode(65, 66, 67) returns 'ABC'.

questions.question: Which method pads the START of a string with another string until reaching a target length (e.g. '5'.padStart(3, '0') -> '005')?
questions.b: str.padStart()
questions.explanation: str.padStart(targetLength, padString) pads the beginning of a string to a given length.

questions.question: Which method pads the END of a string to reach a target length (e.g. 'Hi'.padEnd(5, '!'))?
questions.b: str.padEnd()
questions.explanation: str.padEnd(5, '!') produces 'Hi!!!'.

questions.question: Which method returns a new string containing the specified number of copies of the original string concatenated together?
questions.b: str.repeat()
questions.explanation: 'ha'.repeat(3) returns 'hahaha'.

questions.question: Are primitive strings in JavaScript mutable or immutable?
questions.a: Mutable: characters can be changed with str[0] = 'H'
questions.b: Immutable: string methods always return brand-new strings; individual characters cannot be mutated in place
questions.explanation: JavaScript strings are completely immutable. Any attempt to modify str[0] fails silently (or throws in strict mode).

questions.question: What are Tagged Template Literals in advanced JavaScript (e.g. customTag`Hello ${name}`)?
questions.b: A syntax that allows parsing template literals with a custom function, receiving raw string arrays and evaluated expression arguments
questions.explanation: Tagged templates pass literal chunks and values to a tag function (widely used in libraries like styled-components and graphql).

questions.question: What is String.raw used for as a template tag (e.g. String.raw`C:\new\folder`)?
questions.b: Obtains raw string content without processing backslash escape sequences
questions.explanation: String.raw preserves raw backslashes without evaluating escape characters like \n or \t.

questions.question: Which method concatenates two or more strings together to form a new string?
questions.b: str.concat()
questions.explanation: str.concat(str2, str3) joins multiple strings (though the '+' operator and template literals are more idiomatic).

questions.question: What are the 8 fundamental 'falsy' values in modern JavaScript?
questions.b: false, 0, "false", [], {}, null
questions.explanation: The falsy values in JS are: false, 0, -0, 0n, "" (empty string), null, undefined, and NaN. All other values (including [] and {}) are truthy.

questions.question: What does 'Boolean([])' evaluate to in JavaScript?
questions.b: true (all objects and arrays are truthy, even when empty)
questions.explanation: Empty arrays [] and empty objects {} are objects, which are always truthy in JavaScript.

questions.question: What does 'Boolean("false")' evaluate to?
questions.b: true (non-empty strings are always truthy)
questions.explanation: Any non-empty string, even "false" or "0", evaluates to true when converted to a boolean.

questions.question: What is the result of 'null == undefined' vs 'null === undefined'?
questions.b: false and false
questions.explanation: null == undefined evaluates to true (loose equality coercion), but null === undefined is false (different primitive types).

questions.question: What does the Logical AND operator '&&' evaluate to in expressions like 'A && B'?
questions.b: Returns the first falsy operand if found; otherwise returns the last operand (B)
questions.explanation: In JavaScript, logical operators return the actual operand value: A && B returns A if A is falsy, otherwise B.

questions.question: What does the Logical OR operator '||' evaluate to in expressions like 'A || B'?
questions.a: Returns the first truthy operand if found; otherwise returns the last operand (B)
questions.b: Always returns true
questions.c: Returns null if both are truthy
questions.explanation: A || B returns the first truthy operand; if all are falsy, it returns the final operand.

questions.question: What is Short-Circuit Evaluation in JavaScript logical expressions?
questions.b: Stopping the evaluation of an expression as soon as the outcome is determined (e.g. if left operand of && is falsy, right is never evaluated)
questions.d: An error caused by infinite if statements
questions.explanation: Short-circuiting skips evaluating remaining expressions once the outcome is guaranteed (useful for guarding function calls).

questions.question: What is the Double Bang (!!) operator idiom used for (e.g. !!user)?
questions.b: Explicitly casts/converts any truthy or falsy value into its strict primitive boolean representation (true or false)
questions.explanation: !!value negates the value twice, effectively converting any value into a true boolean.

questions.question: What does 'Object.is(NaN, NaN)' evaluate to in ES6?
questions.b: true
questions.explanation: Object.is() provides same-value equality: Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true, and Object.is(+0, -0) is false.

questions.question: What does 'Object.is(+0, -0)' evaluate to?
questions.b: false
questions.explanation: Unlike === (which considers +0 === -0 true), Object.is distinguishes signed zeros and returns false.

questions.question: What is the standard syntax for an 'if...else if...else' conditional chain?
questions.b: if (c1) { } else if (c2) { } else { }
questions.explanation: JavaScript uses 'if (...) { } else if (...) { } else { }' for sequential conditional branches.

questions.question: What is the result of comparing strings alphabetically with relational operators (e.g. 'apple' < 'banana')?
questions.b: true (strings are compared character-by-character based on Unicode/ASCII code values)
questions.explanation: String comparisons use lexicographical order based on UTF-16 code units ('a' has a lower code than 'b').

questions.question: What does '"12" < "2"' evaluate to in JavaScript?
questions.b: true (because '1' comes before '2' lexicographically in character comparison)
questions.explanation: When comparing two strings, lexicographical comparison compares the first characters: '1' < '2' is true.

questions.question: What does '"12" < 2' evaluate to?
questions.b: false (when comparing a string to a number, the string is coerced to number: 12 < 2 is false)
questions.explanation: When a number is compared with a string, JavaScript converts the string to a number (12 < 2 -> false).

questions.question: What is the output of: let val = null; let res = val ?? 'default'; console.log(res); ?
questions.b: "default"
questions.explanation: The nullish coalescing operator ?? returns 'default' because val is null.

questions.question: What is the output of: let count = 0; let res = count || 10; console.log(res); ?
questions.explanation: 0 is a falsy value, so the logical OR (||) falls back to the right operand 10.

questions.question: What is the output of: let count = 0; let res = count ?? 10; console.log(res); ?
questions.explanation: 0 is NOT null or undefined, so ?? preserves and returns 0.

questions.question: Can an if statement omit curly braces { } if its body consists of only a single statement?
questions.a: No, braces are strictly mandatory in modern JS
questions.b: Yes, though using braces is recommended for readability and avoiding logic bugs
questions.explanation: Single-line statement bodies do not require braces, though omitting them is discouraged by style guides.

questions.question: What does 'false == 0' evaluate to?
questions.b: true
questions.explanation: Loose equality coerces false to number 0, so 0 == 0 is true.

questions.question: What does 'false === 0' evaluate to?
questions.b: false (different types: boolean vs number)
questions.explanation: Strict equality checks types without coercion; boolean is not number, evaluating to false.

questions.question: What does '"" == 0' evaluate to?
questions.b: true (empty string converts to 0 during loose comparison)
questions.explanation: Loose equality coerces empty string "" to number 0, making 0 == 0 true.

questions.question: What does '"" === 0' evaluate to?
questions.b: false
questions.explanation: Strict equality evaluates to false immediately due to differing types (string vs number).

questions.question: What does '[0] == true' evaluate to?
questions.b: false (because [0] coerces to '0' then to number 0; true coerces to 1; 0 == 1 is false)
questions.explanation: [0] converts to "0" -> 0, while true converts to 1, evaluating 0 == 1 to false.

questions.question: What does '[1] == true' evaluate to?
questions.b: true ([1] converts to "1" -> 1; true converts to 1; 1 == 1 is true)
questions.explanation: [1] stringifies to "1" and numericizes to 1; true is 1; 1 == 1 is true.

questions.question: What does the expression 'true ? "A" : false ? "B" : "C"' evaluate to?
questions.explanation: The first condition 'true' is met, returning "A" immediately without evaluating nested branches.

questions.question: What is the result of 'false ? "A" : true ? "B" : "C"'?
questions.explanation: First ternary is false, falling through to the second ternary which evaluates to "B".

questions.question: What does 'Boolean(new Boolean(false))' evaluate to?
questions.b: true (because new Boolean() creates an object wrapper, and all objects are truthy)
questions.explanation: Constructing boolean objects with 'new Boolean(false)' yields an object instance, which is always truthy!

questions.question: What does 'Boolean(Symbol(""))' evaluate to?
questions.b: true
questions.explanation: All Symbol instances are truthy, even if created with an empty description.

questions.question: What does 'Boolean(0n)' evaluate to?
questions.b: false (BigInt zero is falsy)
questions.explanation: 0n (BigInt zero) is one of the 8 standard falsy primitives in JavaScript.

questions.question: What does 'Boolean(1n)' evaluate to?
questions.b: true
questions.explanation: Any non-zero BigInt is truthy.

questions.question: What type of equality comparison does the JavaScript 'switch' statement use to match case expressions?
questions.b: Strict equality (===)
questions.explanation: The switch statement evaluates expressions using strict equality ('===') without type coercion.

questions.question: What happens if a 'break;' statement is omitted at the end of a matching case block in a switch statement?
questions.b: Execution falls through into the subsequent case blocks regardless of whether their criteria match
questions.explanation: Omitting break causes Fall-Through, executing subsequent cases sequentially until a break or switch exit is reached.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'default:' clause in a switch statement?
questions.a: It defines the initial case before any evaluations
questions.b: It executes when none of the case values match the expression
questions.c: It resets all variables in the switch
questions.d: It forces the switch to loop continuously
questions.explanation: The 'default:' case acts as a fallback branch executed when no specific case matches.

questions.question: Is the 'default:' case required to be placed at the very end of the switch block?
questions.a: Yes, syntax rules mandate placing it last
questions.b: No, default can be placed anywhere inside the switch block (though placed at the end by convention)
questions.c: It must always be placed first
questions.d: It can only be placed between case 1 and case 2
questions.explanation: default can appear anywhere in the switch body; if placed earlier without a break, execution falls through.

questions.question: How can multiple case labels share the same block of code in a switch statement?
questions.a: By separating values with commas (e.g. case 1, 2:)
questions.b: By stacking case clauses on top of each other without break statements (e.g. case 'A': case 'B': ...)
questions.explanation: Stacking case labels sequentially leverages deliberate fall-through to execute common logic.

questions.question: What occurs if you declare a 'let' or 'const' variable inside a case block without enclosing braces '{ }'?
questions.a: The variable is only accessible in that case
questions.b: The variable is scoped to the entire switch block, causing duplicate identifier errors if declared in another case
questions.c: It creates a global window variable
questions.d: It compiles without any scope issues
questions.explanation: The whole switch body forms a single lexical scope. Enclosing case logic in '{ ... }' creates an isolated block scope.

questions.question: What is the output of: let x = '5'; switch(x) { case 5: console.log('Num'); break; case '5': console.log('Str'); break; } ?
questions.b: "Str"
questions.explanation: Switch uses strict equality ('==='): '5' === 5 is false, while '5' === '5' is true.

questions.question: Can switch expressions evaluate complex pattern conditions using 'switch(true)'?
questions.a: No, switch only accepts single variables
questions.b: Yes, 'switch(true)' allows each case to evaluate a boolean expression (e.g. case score >= 90:)
questions.explanation: The 'switch(true)' pattern is a clean alternative to long if-else if chains for range comparisons.

questions.question: What does the 'throw' statement do in JavaScript control flow?
questions.b: Generates a user-defined exception, interrupting normal execution flow and passing control to the nearest catch block
questions.c: Throws an element out of an array
questions.explanation: The throw statement raises a runtime exception object (e.g. throw new Error('Invalid input')).

questions.question: What are the three structural blocks of JavaScript exception handling?
questions.b: attempt, handle, complete
questions.explanation: 'try { ... } catch (err) { ... } finally { ... }' provides structured error handling in JavaScript.

questions.question: When does the 'finally' block execute in a try...catch...finally structure?
questions.a: Only if an error was thrown and caught
questions.b: Always, regardless of whether an error was thrown, caught, or even if the try/catch returned early
questions.c: Only if NO errors were thrown
questions.explanation: The 'finally' block is guaranteed to execute after try and catch blocks finish, even if a 'return' statement was encountered.

questions.question: What is Optional Catch Binding introduced in ES2019?
questions.b: Allowing the 'catch' block parameter to be omitted if the error object itself is not needed (e.g. try { ... } catch { ... })
questions.explanation: ES2019 allows writing 'catch { ... }' without declaring an unused '(error)' identifier binding.

questions.question: What standard properties does an Error instance created with 'new Error('Failed')' contain?
questions.b: code and status
questions.explanation: Standard Error objects have 'name' (e.g. 'Error', 'TypeError'), 'message', and a non-standard 'stack' trace.

questions.question: Which built-in error type is thrown when attempting to access a variable that has not been declared?
questions.b: ReferenceError
questions.explanation: ReferenceError indicates that an invalid dereferenced identifier was accessed.

questions.question: Which built-in error type is thrown when a value is not of the expected type (e.g. invoking null as a function: null())?
questions.b: TypeError
questions.explanation: TypeError is thrown when an operation cannot be performed on a value because of an incompatible data type.

questions.question: Which error type is thrown when a numeric value is outside its allowable range (e.g. new Array(-5) or exceeding stack depth)?
questions.b: BoundsError
questions.explanation: RangeError occurs when a value is not within the set or range of allowed values.

questions.question: Which error type is thrown when passing invalid characters to encodeURI() or decodeURI()?
questions.b: TypeError
questions.explanation: URIError is thrown when global URI handling functions are given a malformed URI string.

questions.question: What is Error Cause chaining introduced in ES2022 (e.g. new Error('Failed', { cause: originalErr }))?
questions.b: A standard property linking a new high-level error to the lower-level underlying error that caused it for improved diagnostics
questions.c: A tool to prevent errors from crashing Node.js
questions.explanation: Error causes ({ cause: err }) provide error causality tracking and inspection across abstraction layers.

questions.question: What does the 'return' statement do when executed inside a function body?
questions.b: Stops function execution immediately and returns a specified value (or undefined if no value given) to the caller
questions.d: Returns focus to the browser window
questions.explanation: 'return' terminates function execution and supplies the resulting value to the calling expression.

questions.question: What is returned by a function that reaches the end of its body without executing any 'return' statement?
questions.b: undefined
questions.explanation: In JavaScript, functions without an explicit return statement implicitly return 'undefined'.

questions.question: What is a 'Labelled Statement' in JavaScript (e.g. outerLoop: for (...))?
questions.a: A comment attached to a variable
questions.b: A statement prefixed with an identifier label, allowing 'break <label>' or 'continue <label>' to jump directly out of nested loops
questions.c: A form input label in HTML
questions.explanation: Labels (labelName: loop) allow break and continue statements to target specific outer nested loops.

questions.question: Can 'break' be used to jump out of a labelled plain '{ ... }' block (non-loop)?
questions.a: No, break only works in loops and switch statements
questions.b: Yes, 'break <label>;' can legally break out of any labelled compound block statement
questions.explanation: In JavaScript, 'break labelName;' can exit any labelled block statement.

questions.question: What does the following code return: function test() { try { return 1; } finally { return 2; } } console.log(test()); ?
questions.explanation: A return statement in a 'finally' block overrides any previous return or thrown exception in try/catch.

questions.question: What is the effect of calling 'eval()' in JavaScript, and why is it strongly discouraged?
questions.b: It evaluates arbitrary strings as executable JavaScript code, introducing massive security vulnerabilities (XSS) and destroying engine optimizations
questions.explanation: 'eval()' executes arbitrary code with caller privileges, posing severe security risks and preventing JIT optimizations.

questions.question: What happens if a switch expression does not match any case and no default clause is provided?
questions.b: Execution simply skips the switch statement entirely and proceeds to the following line of code
questions.c: It executes the first case automatically
questions.explanation: If no case matches and default is omitted, execution passes directly to the statement after the switch.

questions.question: Can case values in a switch statement be variable expressions or function calls?
questions.a: No, they must be literal constants only
questions.b: Yes, JavaScript allows arbitrary expressions for case values evaluated dynamically at runtime
questions.explanation: JavaScript evaluates switch case expressions dynamically in top-to-bottom order.

questions.question: What does 'typeof (()=>{})' evaluate to in JavaScript?
questions.b: "function"
questions.explanation: Arrow functions return 'function' from the typeof operator.

questions.question: What is the purpose of re-throwing an error inside a catch block (e.g. catch (err) { log(err); throw err; })?
questions.b: To perform local handling (such as logging or clean-up) while allowing the error to continue propagating up the call stack to higher-level handlers
questions.c: To convert the error to a warning
questions.explanation: Re-throwing preserves error propagation after performing local actions like telemetry logging.

questions.question: What does window.onerror or process.on('uncaughtException') do?
questions.b: Acts as a top-level global fallback error handler catching unhandled exceptions across the entire application
questions.explanation: Global uncaught exception handlers capture runtime errors that were not caught by local try/catch blocks.

questions.question: Can a switch statement switch on boolean or object values in JavaScript?
questions.a: No, only integers and strings are allowed
questions.b: Yes, JavaScript switch statements can evaluate any data type (strings, numbers, booleans, objects)
questions.explanation: JavaScript switch constructs accept any valid data type and evaluate match via strict equality.

questions.question: What is the standard syntax for a traditional 'for' loop in JavaScript?
questions.b: for (i in range(10)) { ... }
questions.explanation: The standard for loop takes initialization, condition, and increment/step expressions separated by semicolons.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between a 'while' loop and a 'do...while' loop?
questions.b: A 'do...while' loop always executes its body at least ONCE before evaluating the condition; a 'while' loop tests condition first
questions.explanation: do...while is an exit-controlled loop that executes the loop body before checking the test expression.

questions.question: What is the 'for...in' loop primarily used for in JavaScript?
questions.a: Iterating directly over values of iterable objects (Arrays, Sets, Maps)
questions.b: Iterating over all enumerable string property keys of an object (including inherited prototype properties)
questions.explanation: for...in iterates over enumerable property keys (names) of an object.

questions.question: What is the 'for...of' loop (introduced in ES6) primarily used for?
questions.b: Iterating directly over the VALUES of iterable objects (Arrays, Strings, Sets, Maps, NodeLists)
questions.explanation: for...of iterates over the values of any iterable object implementing the Symbol.iterator protocol.

questions.question: What happens if you use 'for...of' on a plain JavaScript object (e.g. for (let x of { a: 1, b: 2 }))?
questions.b: It throws a TypeError: object is not iterable
questions.explanation: Plain objects do not implement Symbol.iterator by default, so attempting for...of throws a TypeError. (Use Object.entries() or Object.keys()).

questions.question: How can you safely iterate over an object's entries (key and value) using 'for...of'?
questions.b: for (const item of obj.items())
questions.explanation: Object.entries(obj) returns an array of [key, value] pairs that can be iterated and destructured with for...of.

questions.question: What does the 'break' statement do inside a loop body?
questions.a: Skips the current iteration and jumps to the next step
questions.b: Terminates the loop immediately and transfers control to the statement following the loop
questions.explanation: 'break;' exits the innermost active loop entirely.

questions.question: What does the 'continue' statement do inside a loop body?
questions.b: Skips the remaining statements in the current iteration and advances execution to the next iteration
questions.explanation: 'continue;' immediately terminates the current iteration and steps to the next cycle.

questions.question: What constitutes an intentional infinite loop in JavaScript 'for' syntax?
questions.b: for (null; null; null) { ... }
questions.explanation: for (;;) creates an infinite loop with empty initialization, condition (default true), and step clauses.

questions.question: Why is 'for...in' generally discouraged for iterating over Arrays?
questions.a: It cannot read arrays with more than 5 elements
questions.b: It iterates over array indices as strings, may iterate in arbitrary order, and includes custom enumerable prototype properties
questions.explanation: for...in returns string indices ("0", "1"), visits non-numeric properties, and has no guaranteed iteration order.

questions.question: What does 'for (let char of "Hello")' do?
questions.b: Iterates over each individual character/code point in the string ('H', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o')
questions.explanation: Strings are iterable; for...of iterates over each Unicode character/glyph.

questions.question: What is the 'for await...of' loop used for in modern JavaScript (ES2018)?
questions.a: Iterating through synchronous arrays with 10ms delays
questions.b: Iterating over Async Iterables or streams of Promises sequentially as each promise resolves
questions.explanation: 'for await (const chunk of asyncIterable)' iterates over asynchronous streams and async iterators.

questions.question: Can 'break' and 'continue' statements be used inside an Array.prototype.forEach() callback function?
questions.b: No, using break/continue inside forEach causes a SyntaxError; use return to exit the callback or use a for...of loop
questions.explanation: forEach takes a callback function; break/continue are illegal inside standard function bodies.

questions.question: What method on Object returns an array of an object's own enumerable property names?
questions.b: Object.keys(obj)
questions.explanation: Object.keys(obj) returns an array of string keys for the object's own enumerable properties.

questions.question: What method on Object returns an array of an object's own enumerable property values?
questions.b: Object.values(obj)
questions.explanation: Object.values(obj) returns an array of values corresponding to the object's own enumerable keys.

questions.question: What method checks if a specific property belongs directly to an object (not inherited via prototype chain)?
questions.b: Object.hasOwn(obj, 'prop') or obj.hasOwnProperty('prop')
questions.explanation: Object.hasOwn(obj, prop) (ES2022) and hasOwnProperty verify if a property is an own property of the instance.

questions.question: How many times does the loop 'for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++)' execute its body?
questions.explanation: The loop runs for i = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, which is exactly 5 iterations.

questions.question: How many times does the loop 'let x = 10; do { x++; } while (x < 5);' execute?
questions.b: 1 time (x becomes 11, condition 11 < 5 is false)
questions.explanation: A do...while loop body always executes at least once before checking the condition.

questions.question: What is the output of: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { if (i === 1) continue; console.log(i); } ?
questions.explanation: When i is 1, 'continue' skips the console.log statement, outputting 0 and 2.

questions.question: What is the output of: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { if (i === 1) break; console.log(i); } ?
questions.explanation: When i reaches 1, 'break' exits the loop immediately, so only 0 is logged.

questions.question: What is an Iterator in JavaScript?
questions.b: An object defining a .next() method which returns an object with { value: any, done: boolean }
questions.explanation: The Iterator protocol defines an object with a next() method returning { value, done }.

questions.question: What well-known Symbol must an object implement to be consumable by 'for...of' loops?
questions.b: Symbol.iterator
questions.explanation: An object must have a method at [Symbol.iterator]() returning an iterator object.

questions.question: What is a Generator function in JavaScript?
questions.a: A function that generates random numbers
questions.b: A special function declared with 'function*' that can pause execution using 'yield' and resume later, producing an Iterator
questions.c: A tool that generates HTML markup from templates
questions.d: A function running inside a Web Worker
questions.explanation: function* defines a generator that yields values sequentially and maintains internal execution state across calls.

questions.question: What keyword is used inside a generator function to pause execution and output a value?
questions.b: yield
questions.explanation: The 'yield' keyword pauses generator execution and returns a value to the caller.

questions.question: What does 'yield*' (yield-with-asterisk) do inside a generator function?
questions.b: Delegates iteration to another generator or iterable object
questions.explanation: yield* delegates execution to another generator or iterable sequence (e.g. yield* [1, 2, 3]).

questions.question: What is the effect of changing an array's length property to 0 (e.g. arr.length = 0;)?
questions.b: Completely empties and truncates the array in place, deleting all elements
questions.c: Leaves elements intact but hides them
questions.d: Creates a copy of the array
questions.explanation: Setting arr.length = 0 truncates the array in place, wiping all stored elements.

questions.question: What does the following loop do: let arr = [10, 20, 30]; for (let i = arr.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) { ... } ?
questions.b: Iterates backwards (in reverse order) through the array from last element to first
questions.explanation: Starting at length - 1 and decrementing with i-- traverses an array in reverse order.

questions.question: What is the risk of modifying the array length or mutating an array while iterating over it with a standard index loop?
questions.a: No risk, JavaScript adjusts loop indices automatically
questions.b: Skipping elements or processing elements multiple times due to shifting index offsets (Off-by-One errors)
questions.explanation: Mutating (e.g. splice()) during index iteration shifts subsequent element positions, causing elements to be skipped.

questions.question: How can you iterate over the indices AND elements of an array using 'for...of'?
questions.b: for (const index, element of arr)
questions.explanation: arr.entries() returns an iterable of [index, element] pairs perfect for destructuring in for...of loops.

questions.question: Can 'continue' be used in a 'while' loop without causing an infinite loop if the counter is updated after 'continue'?
questions.a: No; if the increment step is placed after continue, the loop will skip the update and loop infinitely on the same value
questions.b: Yes, JavaScript automatically finds and runs the increment
questions.c: While loops do not support continue
questions.explanation: In while loops, jumping with 'continue' before incrementing the counter skips the update step, causing an infinite loop.

questions.question: What is a Function Declaration in JavaScript?
questions.b: function myFunc() { ... } (declared with the function keyword and an identifier, hoisted completely to the top of its scope)
questions.explanation: Function declarations (function foo() {}) are fully hoisted, allowing them to be called before their definition line.

questions.question: What is a Function Expression?
questions.a: A function defined as part of a larger expression, typically assigned to a variable (e.g. const add = function(a, b) { return a + b; };)
questions.b: A function containing mathematical formulas
questions.d: A function that cannot accept arguments
questions.explanation: Function expressions assign an anonymous or named function to a variable and are not hoisted before assignment.

questions.question: What is the syntax for an ES6 Arrow Function?
questions.b: const myFunc = (a, b) => a + b;
questions.explanation: Arrow functions use the '=>' syntax (e.g. (param) => expression).

questions.question: What is the concise body (implicit return) syntax of an arrow function?
questions.b: const square = x => x * x; (omitting curly braces implicitly returns the evaluated expression)
questions.c: const square = x => return x * x;
questions.explanation: When an arrow function body consists of a single expression without '{ }', the result is implicitly returned.

questions.question: How do you implicitly return an object literal from a concise arrow function?
questions.b: const getUser = () => ({ name: 'Alice' }); (wrapping the object literal in parentheses)
questions.explanation: Parentheses '({ ... })' disambiguate an object literal from a function block body.

questions.question: How does the 'this' keyword behave inside an Arrow Function compared to a traditional function?
questions.a: Arrow functions bind 'this' to the global window object in all cases
questions.b: Arrow functions do NOT have their own 'this' binding; they lexically inherit 'this' from the enclosing parent scope
questions.c: Arrow functions have dynamic 'this' determined at runtime by the caller
questions.d: 'this' is undefined in arrow functions always
questions.explanation: Arrow functions lexically capture the 'this' value of the enclosing execution context.

questions.question: Can an Arrow Function be used as a constructor with the 'new' keyword (e.g. new ArrowFunc())?
questions.b: No, arrow functions do not have a [[Construct]] method or prototype property and throw a TypeError: ArrowFunc is not a constructor
questions.explanation: Arrow functions lack internal constructor mechanisms and cannot be instantiated with 'new'.

questions.question: Do Arrow Functions have access to the special 'arguments' object?
questions.b: No, arrow functions do not have their own 'arguments' object (use ES6 Rest parameters ...args instead)
questions.d: Only if passed more than 2 arguments
questions.explanation: Arrow functions do not bind 'arguments'; modern Rest parameters (...args) should be used instead.

questions.question: How do you specify default parameter values in ES6 function definitions?
questions.b: function greet(name : default('Guest')) { ... }
questions.explanation: ES6 supports default parameter values directly in the parameter list (e.g. function fn(x = 10) {}).

questions.question: What is the Rest Parameter syntax in ES6 function declarations (e.g. function sum(...numbers))?
questions.a: An operator that sleeps the function
questions.b: A prefix of three dots '...' on the final parameter that collects an indefinite number of arguments into a real JavaScript Array
questions.c: A tool to reset function state
questions.explanation: Rest parameters (...args) collect remaining arguments into a true Array instance.

questions.question: Can a function have multiple rest parameters or place a rest parameter before other parameters (e.g. function fn(...a, b))?
questions.b: No, a rest parameter must be the last parameter in the function parameter list and there can only be one (throws SyntaxError: Rest parameter must be last)
questions.d: Only if default values are provided
questions.explanation: A rest parameter must strictly be the final parameter in the signature.

questions.question: What is the difference between the Spread Operator and Rest Parameters?
questions.b: Rest parameters COLLECT multiple function arguments into an array; the Spread operator EXPANDS an array/iterable into individual elements
questions.c: Spread is used only on numbers
questions.explanation: Rest gathers elements into a collection; Spread unpacks/expands a collection into elements.

questions.question: What does the Function.prototype.call() method do?
questions.a: Calls a function after a delay
questions.b: Invokes a function with an explicitly specified 'this' value and arguments provided individually (comma-separated: fn.call(thisArg, arg1, arg2))
questions.c: Converts a function to a string
questions.explanation: call(thisArg, arg1, arg2...) executes a function with a custom 'this' context and individual arguments.

questions.question: What is the difference between Function.prototype.call() and Function.prototype.apply()?
questions.a: call() takes arguments as an array; apply() takes arguments as a comma-separated list
questions.b: call() takes arguments as a comma-separated list; apply() takes arguments as an array [arg1, arg2]
questions.c: apply() only works with arrow functions
questions.explanation: call(thisArg, a, b) takes positional arguments; apply(thisArg, [a, b]) accepts arguments as an array.

questions.question: What does the Function.prototype.bind() method do?
questions.b: Returns a BRAND-NEW function that, when invoked, has its 'this' keyword permanently bound to the provided value and optional preset arguments
questions.explanation: bind() creates a bound function with locked 'this' and preset curried arguments without calling it immediately.

questions.question: What is a Higher-Order Function in JavaScript?
questions.a: A function with more than 100 lines of code
questions.b: A function that accepts one or more functions as arguments, or returns a function as its result (e.g. map, filter, reduce)
questions.c: A function that runs in kernel mode
questions.d: A function declared inside a class
questions.explanation: Higher-order functions take functions as parameters or return new functions.

questions.question: What is a Callback Function in JavaScript?
questions.a: A function that makes telephone calls
questions.b: A function passed as an argument to another function, intended to be executed ("called back") at a later time or after an asynchronous task completes
questions.d: A function stored in local storage
questions.explanation: A callback is a function passed into another function to be invoked when an event or action finishes.

questions.question: What is Function Currying in functional JavaScript programming?
questions.b: The technique of translating a function that takes multiple arguments into a sequence of nested functions that each take a single argument: f(a, b, c) -> f(a)(b)(c)
