questions.explanation: Currying transforms f(a,b) into f(a)(b), allowing partial application of arguments.

questions.question: What is a Pure Function in software engineering?
questions.b: A function that always produces the identical output for the same input arguments and causes NO observable side effects (no mutating external state, I/O, etc.)
questions.explanation: Pure functions are deterministic and free of side effects, making code predictable and testable.

questions.question: What is Recursion in JavaScript?
questions.a: A function that calls itself until it reaches a defined base case condition
questions.b: A loop that runs on multiple threads
questions.d: An error in the garbage collector
questions.explanation: Recursion is a programming pattern where a function calls itself to solve subproblems until reaching a base termination case.

questions.question: What fatal runtime error occurs if a recursive function lacks a base case or recurses too deeply?
questions.b: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded (Stack Overflow)
questions.explanation: Infinite recursion exhausts the JS call stack, throwing 'RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded'.

questions.question: What is Memoization in JavaScript performance optimization?
questions.b: An optimization technique that caches the return values of expensive pure function calls based on input arguments to avoid redundant recalculation
questions.explanation: Memoization caches pure function outputs by argument key to deliver O(1) lookups for repeated invocations.

questions.question: What is an Anonymous Function?
questions.a: A function running over Tor network
questions.b: A function created without a specified identifier/name (often used as inline callbacks or IIFEs)
questions.explanation: An anonymous function is a function without an explicit function name (e.g. function() {} or () => {}).

questions.question: What is the 'name' property on a JavaScript function object (e.g. fn.name)?
questions.b: A string containing the declared name of the function (or inferred variable identifier)
questions.c: The file path where the function resides
questions.explanation: fn.name returns the name of the function or inferred variable binding name.

questions.question: What is the 'length' property on a JavaScript function object (e.g. fn.length)?
questions.a: The number of lines of code in the function
questions.b: The number of formal parameters defined in the function signature (excluding rest parameters and parameters with default values)
questions.explanation: fn.length indicates the arity (number of formal required parameters) declared on the function.

questions.question: What happens when you pass more arguments to a function than the number of parameters declared in its signature in JavaScript?
questions.b: Extra arguments are accepted without error and can be accessed via the arguments object or rest parameters
questions.d: Extra arguments are assigned to null
questions.explanation: JavaScript is dynamically typed and tolerant: surplus arguments are accepted gracefully.

questions.question: What happens when you pass fewer arguments than the declared parameter count in JavaScript?
questions.b: The omitted parameters receive the default value 'undefined'
questions.explanation: Unsupplied parameters default to 'undefined' (unless an explicit default parameter is defined).

questions.question: What does the following classic closure code create: function counter() { let c = 0; return () => ++c; } const next = counter(); next(); next(); ?
questions.a: A private state counter returning 1 then 2
questions.b: 0 then 0
questions.explanation: The returned arrow function closes over the private variable 'c', preserving and incrementing state across calls.

questions.question: What is Function Composition in JavaScript (e.g. compose(f, g)(x))?
questions.b: The process of combining two or more functions to produce a new function where the output of each function is passed as input to the next: f(g(x))
questions.explanation: Function composition chains functions together so data flows through a pipeline of transformations.

questions.question: Can JavaScript functions be passed as arguments, assigned to variables, and returned from other functions (First-Class Functions)?
questions.a: No, functions are not objects in JavaScript
questions.b: Yes, functions are First-Class Citizens (First-Class Objects) in JavaScript
questions.explanation: First-class functions treat functions like any other first-class value (numbers, strings, objects).

questions.question: How do you create an object literal in JavaScript?
questions.b: let person = { name: 'Alice', age: 25 };
questions.explanation: Curly braces '{ key: value }' define an object literal in JavaScript.

questions.question: What are the two ways to access properties on a JavaScript object?
questions.b: Arrow notation (obj->name) and Dot notation (obj.name)
questions.explanation: JavaScript supports dot notation (obj.prop) and bracket notation (obj['prop'] / obj[variable]).

questions.question: When is bracket notation (obj[key]) strictly required over dot notation?
questions.a: When property names are in uppercase
questions.b: When property keys contain spaces, hyphens, special characters, or are stored dynamically in variables
questions.explanation: Bracket notation is necessary when property names are dynamic variables (obj[varName]) or contain non-identifier characters (obj['first-name']).

questions.question: What does the 'Object.assign(target, ...sources)' method do?
questions.a: Assigns a class to an object
questions.b: Copies all enumerable own properties from one or more source objects to a target object, returning the target object (shallow copy/merge)
questions.c: Creates a deep recursive clone of the object
questions.explanation: Object.assign() copies own enumerable properties from sources into the target object.

questions.question: How do you merge two objects using the modern ES6 Object Spread syntax?
questions.b: const merged = obj1 + obj2;
questions.explanation: { ...obj1, ...obj2 } shallow-merges properties from obj1 and obj2 into a new object.

questions.question: What is Object Destructuring syntax in ES6?
questions.a: Deleting all properties from an object
questions.b: An expression that unpacks properties from objects into distinct variables: const { name, age } = person;
questions.c: Compressing an object into a string
questions.d: Converting an object to an array
questions.explanation: Destructuring extracts object properties into local variables cleanly.

questions.question: How do you rename a variable during object destructuring (e.g. mapping prop 'name' to variable 'userName')?
questions.b: const { name: userName } = person;
questions.explanation: 'const { name: userName } = person;' extracts the 'name' property into a variable named 'userName'.

questions.question: What does 'Object.create(proto)' do in JavaScript?
questions.a: Creates a blank empty object without any properties
questions.b: Creates a new object using the specified prototype object as the prototype for the newly created object
questions.explanation: Object.create(proto) creates a new object whose [[Prototype]] link points directly to 'proto'.

questions.question: How do you create a pure dictionary object with NO prototype (no toString, hasOwnProperty, or constructor methods)?
questions.b: new Object(false)
questions.explanation: Object.create(null) creates an object with a null prototype (__proto__ is undefined), free from prototype pollution risks.

questions.question: What is the Prototype Chain in JavaScript?
questions.b: The lookup delegation mechanism where property accesses traverse from the object to its prototype, then prototype's prototype, up to Object.prototype and null
questions.explanation: The prototype chain allows objects to inherit properties and methods from prototype objects.

questions.question: What property on an object instance accesses its internal prototype link in modern standards?
questions.b: Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) (or legacy obj.__proto__)
questions.explanation: Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) is the standard method to inspect an object's prototype (__proto__ is legacy accessor).

questions.question: What is the difference between an object's '__proto__' and a constructor function's 'prototype' property?
questions.b: 'prototype' is a property on constructor functions used to build '__proto__' links on instances created with 'new'; '__proto__' is the actual prototype link on the instance
questions.explanation: Constructor.prototype is the blueprint object assigned to the [[Prototype]] (__proto__) of all instances made with 'new Constructor()'.

questions.question: What does the method 'Object.defineProperty(obj, prop, descriptor)' do?
questions.b: Defines a new property or modifies an existing property on an object with precise control over descriptors (writable, enumerable, configurable, get, set)
questions.explanation: Object.defineProperty() provides granular control over property attributes (enumerable, writable, configurable, getters/setters).

questions.question: What does the 'enumerable' property descriptor attribute control?
questions.a: Whether the property value can be modified
questions.b: Whether the property shows up during enumeration (in for...in loops and Object.keys())
questions.c: Whether the property can be deleted
questions.d: Whether the property holds a number
questions.explanation: If enumerable is false, the property is hidden from for...in loops, Object.keys(), and JSON.stringify().

questions.question: What does the 'writable' property descriptor attribute control?
questions.a: Whether the property can be logged to file
questions.b: Whether the value associated with the property can be changed using an assignment operator
questions.c: Whether the property can be read
questions.d: Whether the property can be sent over HTTP
questions.explanation: If writable is false, assignment to the property fails (or throws TypeError in strict mode).

questions.question: What does the 'configurable' property descriptor attribute control?
questions.a: Whether the property can be saved in config.json
questions.b: Whether the property can be deleted from the object and whether its descriptor attributes can be modified
questions.d: Whether the property is a function
questions.explanation: If configurable is false, the property cannot be deleted with 'delete' and descriptor attributes cannot be changed.

questions.question: What are Getter and Setter methods in JavaScript objects?
questions.a: Methods that fetch data from APIs
questions.b: Accessor properties (get prop() / set prop(val)) that bind object properties to functions executed when getting or setting that property
questions.explanation: Getters ('get') and setters ('set') execute custom validation or computation when properties are read or written.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'Object.seal(obj)' and 'Object.freeze(obj)'?
questions.a: Object.freeze() allows modifying existing values; Object.seal() does not
questions.b: Object.seal() prevents adding/deleting properties but ALLOWS modifying existing writable properties; Object.freeze() prevents adding, deleting, AND modifying properties
questions.explanation: Sealed objects allow mutating existing writable properties; frozen objects make all properties read-only.

questions.question: What does 'Object.isFrozen(obj)' check?
questions.a: Checks if the browser tab is frozen
questions.b: Determines if an object is frozen with Object.freeze()
questions.c: Checks if the code has stopped running
questions.explanation: Object.isFrozen(obj) returns true if the object is frozen.

questions.question: What does 'Object.preventExtensions(obj)' do?
questions.b: Prevents new properties from ever being added to the object (while existing properties can still be modified or deleted)
questions.explanation: Object.preventExtensions(obj) marks an object so that new properties can never be added to it.

questions.question: What does the global 'structuredClone(obj)' function do in modern JavaScript (HTML5 / Node 17+)?
questions.b: Creates a deep, recursive clone of an object including circular references, Maps, Sets, Dates, and TypedArrays
questions.explanation: structuredClone() is the standard algorithm for deep cloning complex nested objects, Sets, Dates, and circular graphs.

questions.question: What is the classic limitation of 'JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))' for deep cloning objects?
questions.b: It loses Functions, undefined, Symbols, RegExps, Dates (converted to strings), and crashes on circular references
questions.explanation: JSON cloning fails on Dates, undefined, functions, BigInts, and circular object graphs.

questions.question: What does 'JSON.stringify(obj, replacer, space)' do in JavaScript?
questions.b: Converts a JavaScript value or object into a formatted JSON text string
questions.explanation: JSON.stringify() serializes a JavaScript object into a standard JSON string format.

questions.question: What does 'JSON.parse(jsonString)' do in JavaScript?
questions.a: Converts an object into a JSON string
questions.b: Parses a JSON string and constructs the corresponding JavaScript value or object
questions.explanation: JSON.parse() deserializes a JSON string into living JavaScript objects and data types.

questions.question: What is Shorthand Property Names syntax in ES6 object literals (e.g. const name = 'Alice'; const obj = { name };)?
questions.b: It automatically uses the variable name as the property key and the variable value as the property value ({ name: name })
questions.explanation: If key and variable name match, { name } is shorthand for { name: name }.

questions.question: What is Computed Property Names syntax in ES6 object literals (e.g. { [propName]: 42 })?
questions.b: Using square brackets inside an object literal to compute the property key dynamically from an expression
questions.d: A tool to sort object keys
questions.explanation: [expression]: value allows dynamic evaluation of object keys at creation time.

questions.question: What is Shorthand Method Definitions syntax in ES6 object literals?
questions.b: sayHello() { ... } (omitting the ': function' keyword)
questions.explanation: ES6 allows concise method declarations: { greet() { return 'Hi'; } }.

questions.question: What is Prototype Pollution in JavaScript security?
questions.b: A vulnerability where an attacker injects properties into Object.prototype via unvalidated keys (like '__proto__' or 'constructor.prototype'), affecting all objects in the runtime
questions.explanation: Prototype pollution modifies Object.prototype, injecting malicious properties into all objects across the application.

questions.question: What does 'Object.fromEntries(iterable)' do in ES2019?
questions.b: Transforms a list of key-value pairs (like an array of entries or a Map) into an object (the reverse of Object.entries())
questions.explanation: Object.fromEntries([['a', 1], ['b', 2]]) constructs the object { a: 1, b: 2 }.

questions.question: What is the return value of 'Object.getOwnPropertyNames(obj)'?
questions.b: An array of ALL own string properties found directly upon a given object, including non-enumerable properties
questions.explanation: Object.getOwnPropertyNames() returns all string property keys (both enumerable and non-enumerable) directly on the object.

questions.question: Which method adds one or more elements to the END of an array and returns the new length of the array?
questions.b: arr.push()
questions.explanation: arr.push(element) appends elements to the end of an array in place and returns its updated length.

questions.question: Which method removes the LAST element from an array and returns that removed element?
questions.b: arr.pop()
questions.explanation: arr.pop() removes and returns the last element, mutating the array in place.

questions.question: Which method adds one or more elements to the BEGINNING of an array and returns the new length?
questions.b: arr.unshift()
questions.explanation: arr.unshift(element) inserts elements at index 0 and shifts subsequent elements to the right.

questions.question: Which method removes the FIRST element from an array and returns that removed element?
questions.b: arr.shift()
questions.explanation: arr.shift() removes and returns the element at index 0, shifting subsequent indices left.

questions.question: What is the critical difference between Array.prototype.slice() and Array.prototype.splice()?
questions.a: slice() mutates the original array; splice() does not
questions.b: slice() returns a shallow copy of a portion of an array without modifying the original; splice() modifies the original array in place by removing/replacing elements
questions.explanation: slice() is non-mutating (returns a new sub-array); splice() is mutating (modifies the array in place).

questions.question: What does 'arr.map(callback)' do in JavaScript?
questions.b: Creates a brand-new array populated with the results of calling a provided callback function on every element in the calling array
questions.c: Mutates the original array in place
questions.explanation: map() transforms each element via a callback and returns a new array of identical length.

questions.question: What does 'arr.filter(callback)' do in JavaScript?
questions.b: Creates a shallow copy of a portion of the array filtered down to only the elements that pass the truth test implemented by the callback function
questions.explanation: filter() returns a new array containing all elements for which the callback returns a truthy value.

questions.question: What does 'arr.reduce(callback, initialValue)' do in JavaScript?
questions.b: Executes a reducer callback function on each element of the array in order, accumulating a single resulting output value (e.g. sum, object)
questions.explanation: reduce((acc, curr) => ..., init) accumulates elements into a single aggregate value.

questions.question: What does 'arr.find(callback)' return?
questions.a: An array of all matching elements
questions.b: The value of the FIRST element in the array that satisfies the provided testing function, or undefined if not found
questions.c: The index of the matching element
questions.explanation: find() returns the first item matching the predicate condition, or undefined if no elements match.

questions.question: What does 'arr.findIndex(callback)' return?
questions.a: The index of the FIRST element that satisfies the testing function, or -1 if no match is found
questions.b: The element value itself
questions.explanation: findIndex() returns the 0-based index of the first matching element, or -1.

questions.question: Which ES2023 methods find the LAST matching element or its index in an array?
questions.b: arr.reverseFind() and arr.reverseIndex()
questions.explanation: findLast() and findLastIndex() (ES2023) iterate in reverse order to find the last satisfying item.

questions.question: What does 'arr.some(callback)' return?
questions.b: true if AT LEAST ONE element in the array passes the condition implemented by the callback function; otherwise false
questions.explanation: some() tests whether at least one element in the array satisfies the predicate function.

questions.question: What does 'arr.every(callback)' return?
questions.b: true if ALL elements in the array pass the condition implemented by the callback function; otherwise false
questions.explanation: every() tests whether all elements in the array pass the provided test function.

questions.question: What does 'arr.includes(value)' return?
questions.b: true if the array contains the specified value (using SameValueZero algorithm, correctly finding NaN); otherwise false
questions.explanation: includes() determines whether an array includes a certain value, returning true or false (and safely detects NaN).

questions.question: How does 'arr.sort()' behave by default when no comparator function is supplied?
questions.a: Sorts numbers in ascending numeric order (1, 2, 10, 20)
questions.b: Converts elements to strings and sorts them in ascending UTF-16 character code lexicographical order (producing [1, 10, 2, 20])
questions.explanation: Default sort() converts elements to strings, sorting alphabetically (e.g. 10 comes before 2).

questions.question: How do you sort an array of numbers in ascending numerical order correctly?
questions.b: numbers.sort((a, b) => a - b)
questions.explanation: numbers.sort((a, b) => a - b) provides a custom comparator that correctly orders numbers ascendingly.

questions.question: Which ES2023 non-mutating methods return new arrays instead of modifying the original array in place?
questions.b: sortCopy(), reverseCopy(), spliceCopy()
questions.explanation: ES2023 introduced toSorted(), toReversed(), toSpliced(), and with() to perform operations immutably without mutating the source array.

questions.question: What does 'arr.flat(depth)' do in ES2019?
questions.b: Creates a new array with all sub-array elements concatenated into it recursively up to the specified depth
questions.d: Converts an array into a flat string
questions.explanation: flat(depth) flattens nested arrays (e.g. [1, [2, [3]]].flat(2) becomes [1, 2, 3]).

questions.question: What does 'arr.flatMap(callback)' do in ES2019?
questions.a: Maps an array to an object
questions.b: Identical to calling .map(callback) followed by .flat(1) in a single optimized pass
questions.explanation: flatMap() maps each element using a mapping function and flattens the result into a new array by 1 level.

questions.question: What does 'Array.from(iterable, mapFn)' do?
questions.b: Creates a new, shallow-copied Array instance from an iterable or array-like object (such as arguments, NodeList, or Set)
questions.c: Imports an array from a file
questions.d: Checks if a variable is an array
questions.explanation: Array.from() converts array-like objects (e.g. document.querySelectorAll) and iterables into genuine Array instances.

questions.question: How do you test if a variable 'x' is a genuine Array in JavaScript?
questions.b: Array.isArray(x)
questions.explanation: Array.isArray(x) reliably checks if an object is an Array across iframes and execution realms.

questions.question: What does 'arr.join(separator)' do?
questions.b: Concatenates all elements of an array into a string, separated by the specified separator string (defaulting to comma ',')
questions.explanation: join('-') returns a string with all array elements joined by the delimiter (e.g. ['a','b'].join('-') -> 'a-b').

questions.question: What is Array Destructuring syntax in ES6?
questions.b: Unpacking values from an array into individual variables: const [first, second, ...rest] = arr;
questions.d: Converting an array to a set
questions.explanation: const [a, b] = arr allows positional unpacking of array elements into distinct variables.

questions.question: How do you swap two variables 'a' and 'b' in a single line using array destructuring?
questions.explanation: '[a, b] = [b, a];' swaps two variable values cleanly without requiring an intermediate temporary variable.

questions.question: What is a 'Sparse Array' in JavaScript?
questions.b: An array containing empty slots / holes (where array.length is greater than the actual number of populated elements, e.g. [1, , 3])
questions.d: An array that contains only zeros
questions.explanation: Sparse arrays contain empty slots (holes) where indices do not exist as own properties on the array.

questions.question: What does 'arr.fill(value, start, end)' do?
questions.a: Fills missing array indices with null
questions.b: Changes all elements in an array to a static value from start index to end index in place
questions.c: Generates random numbers into an array
questions.explanation: arr.fill(0) fills an array with static values in place (useful for initializing fixed-size arrays).

questions.question: What does 'arr.reverse()' do?
questions.a: Creates a reversed copy of the array
questions.b: Reverses an array IN PLACE, modifying the original array and returning the reference to it
questions.explanation: reverse() mutates the calling array in place (use toReversed() in ES2023 for non-mutating reverse).

questions.question: What does 'Array.of(7)' produce vs 'new Array(7)'?
questions.a: Array.of(7) produces [7]; new Array(7) produces an array with length 7 containing 7 empty slots
questions.b: Both produce [7]
questions.explanation: Array.of() creates an array with the given arguments regardless of number or type, avoiding the new Array(length) pitfall.

questions.question: What does the 'arr.with(index, value)' method do in ES2023?
questions.a: Binds an array to a class
questions.b: Returns a new array with the element at the given index replaced with the given value without modifying the original array
questions.explanation: arr.with(2, 'newVal') returns a new array with updated value at index 2 without mutating arr.

questions.question: What is the return value of '[1, 2, 3].concat([4, 5])'?
questions.explanation: concat() merges arrays into a brand-new combined array.

questions.question: How do you create a Date object representing the current instant in time in JavaScript?
questions.b: new Date()
questions.explanation: new Date() instantiates a Date object initialized to the current date and time.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What does 'Date.now()' return?
questions.b: The number of milliseconds elapsed since the Unix Epoch (January 1, 1970 00:00:00 UTC)
questions.c: The current year as an integer
questions.explanation: Date.now() returns the numeric timestamp in milliseconds since January 1, 1970 UTC.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What is the zero-based indexing quirk of months in the JavaScript Date object (e.g. date.getMonth())?
questions.b: January is 0 and December is 11
questions.d: Months are indexed in roman numerals
questions.explanation: getMonth() returns months from 0 (January) to 11 (December).
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: Which Date method returns the 4-digit year (e.g. 2026)?
questions.b: date.getFullYear()
questions.explanation: date.getFullYear() returns the 4-digit year (getYear() is deprecated and returned year minus 1900).
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: Which Date method formats a date into an ISO 8601 extended format string (e.g. '2026-08-31T10:00:00.000Z')?
questions.b: date.toISOString()
questions.explanation: date.toISOString() returns a universal ISO 8601 formatted timestamp string in UTC.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What is a 'Set' in ES6 JavaScript?
questions.a: An object with fixed property sizes
questions.b: A collection of unique values of any type where each value may occur only once
questions.c: A tool to configure environment variables
questions.explanation: A Set is an ordered collection of unique values where duplicate insertions are automatically discarded.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: How do you quickly remove duplicate elements from an array in modern JavaScript?
questions.b: const unique = [...new Set(arr)];
questions.explanation: '[...new Set(arr)]' converts an array to a Set to strip duplicates, then spreads it back into an array.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: Which method adds a new value to a Set in JavaScript?
questions.b: set.add(val)
questions.explanation: set.add(value) inserts a value into a Set (and returns the Set instance).
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: Which method checks if a value exists inside a Set?
questions.b: set.has(val)
questions.explanation: set.has(value) returns a boolean true/false indicating if the value exists in O(1) time.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: Which property returns the total count of elements in a Set or Map?
questions.b: set.size
questions.explanation: The '.size' property returns the number of elements in a Set or key-value entries in a Map.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What is a 'Map' in ES6 JavaScript?
questions.a: A tool for rendering Google Maps
questions.b: A collection of keyed data items where keys can be of ANY data type (including objects, functions, and primitives)
questions.explanation: A Map is a hash map data structure supporting keys of any type (unlike plain objects where keys are strings/symbols).
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: Which method sets a key-value entry in a Map?
questions.b: map.set(key, val)
questions.explanation: map.set(key, value) sets a key-value pair and returns the Map object.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: Which method retrieves a value by key from a Map?
questions.b: map.get(key)
questions.explanation: map.get(key) returns the value associated with the key, or undefined if the key is not found.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What is a 'WeakMap' in JavaScript?
questions.a: A Map that runs with lower CPU priority
questions.b: A collection of key/value pairs in which the keys MUST be objects and are held weakly, allowing unreferenced key objects to be garbage collected
questions.c: A Map that holds only numbers
questions.d: A Map with a maximum size of 10 items
questions.explanation: WeakMap holds weak references to object keys, preventing memory leaks when managing private metadata.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: Can a WeakMap or WeakSet be iterated over with for...of or have a .size property?
questions.a: Yes, exactly like standard Maps and Sets
questions.b: No, WeakMaps/WeakSets are not iterable and have no .size property because entries can be garbage collected non-deterministically
questions.d: Only if all keys are strings
questions.explanation: Weak collections cannot be iterated or counted because garbage collection makes their contents non-deterministic.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: How do you create a Regular Expression literal in JavaScript?
questions.b: /pattern/flags (e.g. /^[A-Z0-9]+$/i)
questions.explanation: Regex literals are enclosed between forward slashes /pattern/flags.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What does the regular expression flag 'i' specify in /pattern/i?
questions.b: Case-insensitive matching (ignores uppercase vs lowercase differences)
questions.explanation: The 'i' flag enables case-insensitive pattern matching.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What does the regular expression flag 'g' specify in /pattern/g?
questions.a: Global search (matches all occurrences across the string rather than stopping at the first match)
questions.b: Greedy matching only
questions.explanation: The 'g' flag performs a global search, finding all matches in the text.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What does the regular expression flag 'm' specify in /pattern/m?
questions.b: Multiline matching (treats beginning '^' and end '$' characters as matching the start and end of each line)
questions.explanation: The 'm' flag makes '^' and '$' match the beginning and end of each line within a multiline string.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What does the regular expression flag 's' (dotAll) do in ES2018?
questions.b: Allows the dot '.' character to match any character INCLUDING newline characters (\n, \r)
questions.explanation: The 's' (dotAll) flag allows '.' to match newline characters as well.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: Which RegExp method tests for a match in a string and returns a boolean (true or false)?
questions.b: regex.test(str)
questions.explanation: regex.test(str) returns true if the regular expression matches anywhere in the string.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: Which RegExp method executes a search for a match and returns an array of match information or null?
questions.b: regex.exec(str)
questions.explanation: regex.exec(str) returns detailed match information (captures, index, input) or null.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: Which String method searches a string against a regular expression and returns an array of all matches?
questions.b: str.regexSearch()
questions.explanation: str.match(regex) and str.matchAll(regex) retrieve matches and capture groups from a string.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What does the regex character class '\d' match?
questions.b: Any decimal digit character (equivalent to [0-9])
questions.explanation: \d matches any ASCII decimal digit (0-9).
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What does the regex character class '\w' match?
questions.b: Any alphanumeric word character plus underscore (equivalent to [a-zA-Z0-9_])
questions.explanation: \w matches any ASCII alphanumeric character or underscore.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What does the regex character class '\s' match?
questions.b: Any whitespace character (space, tab, form feed, newline)
questions.explanation: \s matches any whitespace character (space, \t, \n, \r).
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What does the quantifier '+' represent in regular expressions?
questions.b: 1 or more occurrences (matching at least once)
questions.explanation: '+' matches 1 or more consecutive occurrences of the preceding token.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What does the quantifier '*' represent in regular expressions?
questions.b: 0 or more occurrences (optional repeat)
questions.d: All characters until end of line
questions.explanation: '*' matches 0 or more occurrences of the preceding token.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What does the quantifier '?' represent in regular expressions?
questions.b: 0 or 1 occurrence (makes the preceding item optional, or makes a greedy quantifier lazy)
questions.explanation: '?' makes the preceding element optional (0 or 1 time) or switches quantifiers to lazy mode.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: What are Named Capture Groups in ES2018 regular expressions (e.g. /(?<year>\d{4})-(?<month>\d{2})/)?
questions.b: Capture groups assigned meaningful identifier names accessible via the match.groups object
questions.d: Tool to export regex to JSON
questions.explanation: Named capture groups (?<name>...) populate match.groups[name] with matched substring values.
questions.moduleName: JS Dates, Sets, Maps & Regular Expressions

questions.question: Which keyword introduced in ES6 defines a class in JavaScript?
questions.b: class
questions.explanation: The 'class' keyword defines a class in JavaScript syntactic sugar over prototypical inheritance.

questions.question: Which special method is invoked automatically when creating a new instance of a class with the 'new' keyword?
questions.b: constructor()
questions.explanation: The 'constructor' method is the special initialization function executed when instantiating a class.

questions.question: Which keyword is used in a class declaration to create a child class that inherits from a parent class?
questions.b: extends
questions.explanation: The 'extends' keyword establishes prototypical inheritance between child and parent classes (e.g. class Dog extends Animal).

questions.question: What must you call inside a derived (subclass) constructor before accessing 'this'?
questions.b: parent()
questions.explanation: Calling 'super(...args)' invokes the parent class constructor and binds the 'this' context for the subclass.

questions.question: What does the 'static' keyword do when applied to a class method or field in JavaScript?
questions.b: Attaches the method/property to the class constructor itself rather than instances of the class (called as ClassName.method())
questions.c: Prevents the method from being overridden
questions.explanation: Static methods and fields belong to the class namespace directly, not to individual instantiated objects.

questions.question: What prefix syntax is used to declare true Private Fields and Methods in ES2022 classes?
questions.b: #myField;
questions.explanation: The hash '#' prefix (e.g. #privateCount = 0;) defines private fields inaccessible outside the class body.

questions.question: What happens if code outside a class attempts to access a private field (e.g. instance.#secret)?
questions.b: Throws a hard SyntaxError at compile time
questions.explanation: Private fields are enforced at language syntax level; accessing them outside class scope throws a SyntaxError.

questions.question: What is a Static Initialization Block in ES2022 classes (e.g. static { ... })?
questions.a: A block that initializes CSS styles
questions.b: A block inside a class body executed once when the class is loaded to evaluate complex static state or share private access
questions.c: A block that runs on server boot
questions.explanation: Static initialization blocks (static { }) run once per class evaluation to configure static properties.

questions.question: Are class declarations hoisted in JavaScript like function declarations?
questions.a: Yes, fully hoisted and callable before definition
questions.b: No, classes are hoisted into the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) and cannot be referenced before declaration (throws ReferenceError)
questions.explanation: Classes exist in the Temporal Dead Zone before their declaration line and cannot be instantiated before defined.

questions.question: Does the body of a JavaScript class execute in Strict Mode by default?
questions.a: No, strict mode must be manually declared with 'use strict'
questions.b: Yes, the code within class bodies is always executed in strict mode automatically
questions.explanation: Class bodies are always evaluated in strict mode automatically per ECMAScript specification.

questions.question: Which keyword exports functions, objects, or values from an ES6 module file?
questions.b: export
questions.explanation: The 'export' keyword exports named or default bindings from an ES module.

questions.question: Which keyword imports bindings from an external ES6 module file?
questions.b: import
questions.explanation: The 'import' keyword loads exported bindings from other modules (e.g. import { add } from './math.js').

questions.question: How many 'export default' declarations can exist per ES6 module file?
questions.b: Exactly ONE default export per module
questions.explanation: A module can have multiple named exports, but at most ONE default export.

questions.question: How do you import a default export from a module file?
questions.b: import MyComponent from './MyComponent.js';
questions.explanation: Default exports are imported without curly braces and can be given any local identifier name.

questions.question: How do you import all named exports from a module under a single namespace alias?
questions.b: import * as Utils from './utils.js';
questions.explanation: import * as Name from './module.js' imports all exports into a namespace object.

questions.question: What is Dynamic Import in JavaScript (e.g. import('./module.js'))?
questions.b: A function-like expression returning a Promise that resolves to the module namespace, enabling on-demand lazy loading of code chunks
questions.d: A tool that converts CommonJS to ES modules
questions.explanation: Dynamic import() returns a promise, enabling code-splitting and conditional lazy loading of modules.

questions.question: What is 'import.meta' in ES Modules?
questions.b: A host-provided object exposing context-specific metadata about the current module (e.g. import.meta.url)
questions.explanation: import.meta exposes module metadata, such as the module's file URL (import.meta.url).

questions.question: What is the difference between ES6 Modules (ESM) and CommonJS (CJS) used in legacy Node.js?
questions.b: ESM uses static 'import/export' analyzed at compile time; CommonJS uses dynamic synchronous 'require()' and 'module.exports' at runtime
questions.explanation: ESM is the official ECMAScript standard with static dependency graphs, while CommonJS is Node's legacy runtime loader.

questions.question: What is Method Overriding in class inheritance?
questions.a: Writing two methods with the same name and different parameters
questions.b: A child class providing its own implementation of a method that is already defined in its parent class (optionally calling super.method())
questions.explanation: Method overriding replaces parent behavior in subclasses, with super.method() used to invoke parent logic.

questions.question: What does the 'super' keyword reference when used inside a method of a class?
questions.b: The prototype object of the parent superclass
questions.explanation: super.methodName() calls the method implementation on the parent superclass prototype.

questions.question: What are Class Fields (Public Instance Fields) in modern JavaScript?
questions.b: Instance properties declared directly in the class body without needing constructor assignment: class User { count = 0; }
questions.explanation: Class fields allow declaring default instance properties directly on the class definition.

questions.question: What is the 'Top-Level Await' feature in modern ES Modules (ES2022)?
questions.a: An error caused by unhandled promises
questions.b: The ability to use the 'await' keyword directly at the top level of an ES module without wrapping it in an async function
questions.c: A tool that freezes page scrolling
questions.explanation: Top-level await enables modules to await asynchronous initialization before dependent modules execute.

questions.question: What is an Abstract Class pattern in JavaScript?
questions.a: A class with an abstract keyword built into JS syntax
questions.b: A base class designed to be inherited from but never instantiated directly (often throwing an error in its constructor if new.target === BaseClass)
questions.d: A class written in TypeScript only
questions.explanation: Abstract classes in JS prevent direct instantiation by checking 'if (new.target === AbstractClass) throw new Error()'.

questions.question: What is 'new.target' in JavaScript constructors and classes?
questions.a: A reference to the next mouse click target
questions.b: A metaproperty that references the constructor function that was invoked with the 'new' operator
questions.explanation: new.target detects whether a function was called with 'new' and identifies the subclass constructor being instantiated.

questions.question: What happens if you attempt to call a class constructor as a normal function without 'new' (e.g. User())?
questions.b: It throws a TypeError: Class constructor User cannot be invoked without 'new'
questions.explanation: Classes cannot be called like regular functions; invoking without 'new' throws a TypeError.

questions.question: What is Polymorphism in object-oriented JavaScript programming?
questions.b: The ability of different classes to define the same method name with custom implementations, allowing them to be treated uniformly through a shared interface
questions.d: Creating multiple variables in one line
questions.explanation: Polymorphism allows distinct subclass types to share a common method signature tailored to each subtype.

questions.question: What is the Mixin pattern in JavaScript class design?
questions.b: A pattern of parameterized class factory functions used to compose multiple reusable method bundles onto classes since JS only supports single inheritance
questions.c: A method to shuffle array items
questions.explanation: Mixins compose functionality across class hierarchies to overcome single inheritance limitations.

questions.question: What is the 'export { x as newName }' syntax used for in ES modules?
questions.a: Renaming an export binding upon export
questions.b: Exporting to a different file path
questions.explanation: 'as' renames exported or imported identifiers (e.g. export { func as publicFunc }).

questions.question: What does 'export * from './module.js'' do (Re-exporting / Aggregation)?
questions.a: Deletes all exports from the target module
questions.b: Re-exports all named exports from the specified module, acting as a unified barrel file entrypoint
questions.explanation: Re-exporting aggregates module exports into unified package entrypoints (barrel files).

questions.question: Are ES Module files automatically executed in Strict Mode?
questions.a: No, 'use strict' must be explicitly declared at line 1
questions.b: Yes, ES Modules are always in Strict Mode by default without needing the 'use strict' directive
questions.explanation: All ES Modules are strictly scoped and execute in strict mode by default.

questions.question: What is the Event Loop in JavaScript runtime architecture?
questions.a: A for loop that checks user clicks
questions.b: The core concurrency mechanism that monitors the Call Stack and Task Queues, pushing callbacks to the stack when it becomes empty
questions.explanation: The Event Loop continuously transfers tasks from Microtask and Callback Queues onto the Call Stack when empty.

questions.question: What is the difference between the Microtask Queue and the Macrotask (Callback) Queue in JavaScript?
questions.b: Microtasks (Promises, queueMicrotask) have higher priority and are completely drained before the Event Loop executes the next macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O)
questions.c: There is no difference in priority
questions.d: Microtasks only run on Web Workers
questions.explanation: The microtask queue is fully processed after each execution task before handling the next macrotask.

questions.question: What are the three possible states of a JavaScript Promise?
questions.b: Pending, Fulfilled (resolved), Rejected
questions.explanation: A Promise is always in one of 3 states: Pending (initial), Fulfilled (success), or Rejected (failure).

questions.question: Which method is used to attach a callback executed when a Promise fulfills with a value?
questions.b: promise.then()
questions.explanation: promise.then(onFulfilled, onRejected) handles successful resolution.

questions.question: Which method is used to attach an error handler callback when a Promise rejects?
questions.b: promise.catch()
questions.explanation: promise.catch(onRejected) handles promise rejections and errors.

questions.question: Which method attaches a callback that executes when a Promise settles (either fulfilled OR rejected)?
questions.b: promise.finally()
questions.explanation: promise.finally(callback) executes clean-up logic once the promise settles in either state.

questions.question: What does the 'async' keyword placed before a function declaration guarantee?
questions.a: The function runs in a separate thread
questions.b: The function automatically returns a Promise (wrapping non-promise return values in Promise.resolve)
questions.explanation: An 'async' function wraps its return value in a Promise and enables the use of 'await' inside its body.

questions.question: What does the 'await' keyword do when placed before a Promise inside an async function?
questions.b: Pauses execution of the async function in a non-blocking manner until the Promise settles, resolving to the fulfilled value or throwing the rejection
questions.d: Converts the promise to a string
questions.explanation: await suspends async function execution until the promise settles, resuming seamlessly upon resolution.

questions.question: How do you handle errors thrown by an 'await' expression inside an async function?
questions.b: Using an if-error statement
questions.c: Errors cannot be caught in async functions
questions.explanation: A standard try...catch block catches rejected promises and errors originating from awaited calls.

questions.question: What does 'Promise.all([p1, p2, p3])' do?
questions.a: Resolves with the first promise that settles
questions.b: Returns a Promise that fulfills with an array of all results when ALL input promises fulfill; rejects IMMEDIATELY if any single promise rejects (fail-fast)
questions.c: Executes promises sequentially one by one
questions.explanation: Promise.all waits for all promises to fulfill, or short-circuits on the first rejection.

questions.question: What does 'Promise.allSettled([p1, p2])' do in ES2020?
questions.b: Waits until ALL promises settle (fulfill or reject) and returns an array of objects describing the outcome of each ({ status: 'fulfilled', value } or { status: 'rejected', reason })
questions.explanation: Promise.allSettled() never short-circuits on rejection, waiting for all promises to conclude.

questions.question: What does 'Promise.race([p1, p2])' do?
questions.a: Returns a promise that fulfills or rejects as soon as the FIRST promise in the iterable settles (with that result/rejection)
questions.b: Runs promises in parallel on multi-core CPUs
questions.explanation: Promise.race() settles with the outcome (fulfillment or rejection) of the fastest promise.

questions.question: What does 'Promise.any([p1, p2])' do in ES2021?
questions.a: Resolves as soon as ANY promise fulfills (ignoring rejections); only rejects (with an AggregateError) if ALL input promises reject
questions.b: Rejects on the first failure
questions.explanation: Promise.any() waits for the first successful fulfillment, ignoring errors unless all fail.

questions.question: What is an AggregateError in JavaScript?
questions.b: An error object that wraps multiple individual errors together (such as when Promise.any() rejects because all input promises failed)
questions.c: A syntax error in math formulas
questions.explanation: AggregateError encapsulates multiple errors in an 'errors' array property.

questions.question: What does the Fetch API 'fetch(url)' function return?
questions.b: A Promise that resolves to a Response object representing the HTTP response
questions.explanation: fetch() returns a Promise resolving to the Response object of the network request.

questions.question: Why does 'fetch()' NOT reject the Promise on HTTP 404 or 500 status codes?
questions.a: Because fetch is broken in modern browsers
questions.b: Because fetch only rejects on actual network failure (DNS error, connection refused); HTTP status codes like 404/500 resolve successfully with 'response.ok === false'
questions.c: Because 404 is considered a success status
questions.explanation: fetch() only rejects on network failures; HTTP error statuses resolve normally with response.ok set to false.

questions.question: How do you parse a JSON body from a Fetch API Response object?
questions.b: const data = await response.json();
questions.explanation: response.json() returns a Promise that reads and parses the response stream as JSON.

questions.question: How do you read a text response from a Fetch API Response object?
questions.b: const text = await response.text();
questions.explanation: response.text() returns a promise resolving with the raw text content.

questions.question: How can you cancel / abort an active 'fetch()' request using standard Web APIs?
questions.b: Using an AbortController instance and passing its signal to fetch({ signal: controller.signal }), then calling controller.abort()
questions.explanation: AbortController and its associated AbortSignal allow programmatic cancellation of fetch requests.

questions.question: What is 'Promise.withResolvers()' introduced in ES2024?
questions.b: A static helper method returning an object containing a new Promise along with its { promise, resolve, reject } functions exposed externally
questions.explanation: Promise.withResolvers() cleanly extracts { promise, resolve, reject } without nesting constructor callbacks.

questions.question: What does 'setTimeout(fn, 0)' do in JavaScript?
questions.a: Executes the function synchronously and immediately
questions.b: Schedules the callback function to run on the next tick of the Event Loop after the current call stack has completely cleared
questions.explanation: setTimeout(..., 0) defers callback execution to the macrotask queue after current synchronous execution finishes.

questions.question: Which method cancels a pending timer scheduled with setTimeout()?
questions.b: clearTimeout(id)
questions.explanation: clearTimeout(timeoutId) cancels a scheduled timer before it executes.

questions.question: Which function repeatedly executes a callback function at a specified fixed interval in milliseconds?
questions.b: setInterval()
questions.explanation: setInterval(callback, intervalMs) repeatedly invokes the callback every intervalMs milliseconds.

questions.question: Which method cancels a recurring timer created with setInterval()?
questions.b: clearInterval(id)
questions.explanation: clearInterval(intervalId) stops the recurring timer from firing again.

questions.question: What is 'Callback Hell' (Pyramid of Doom) in legacy asynchronous JavaScript?
questions.b: Deeply nested, hard-to-read callback functions resulting from chaining multiple asynchronous operations together prior to Promises
questions.explanation: Callback Hell describes pyramid-shaped, nested callback structures that Promises and async/await solve.

questions.question: What is 'queueMicrotask(fn)' in JavaScript?
questions.a: Schedules a function to run after 1 hour
questions.b: Explicitly queues a microtask to be executed at the end of the current turn of the event loop, before rendering or macrotasks
questions.c: A tool for multi-core worker dispatch
questions.explanation: queueMicrotask() explicitly inserts a callback into the high-priority microtask queue.

questions.question: What is an Unhandled Promise Rejection in modern JavaScript environments?
questions.a: A resolved promise with null data
questions.b: A Promise that was rejected without any .catch() handler attached, potentially terminating Node.js processes or logging browser errors
questions.explanation: Failing to attach a catch handler to a rejected promise triggers unhandledrejection events.

questions.question: What HTTP header must be set to send JSON payloads using fetch()?
questions.b: 'Accept-Encoding': 'json'
questions.explanation: Setting headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } notifies the server that the request body is JSON.

questions.question: How do you send a POST request with JSON data using fetch()?
questions.b: fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify(data) })
questions.explanation: POST requests require specifying method: 'POST', Content-Type header, and JSON-stringified body.

questions.question: What is 'Promise.resolve(val)' and 'Promise.reject(reason)'?
questions.a: Static methods that return immediately fulfilled or immediately rejected Promise objects
questions.b: Methods that reset the event loop
questions.explanation: Promise.resolve(val) and Promise.reject(err) generate settled promises instantly.

questions.question: Which document method returns the first DOM element matching a specified CSS selector string?
questions.b: document.querySelector()
questions.explanation: document.querySelector(selector) returns the first matching element, or null if none match.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: Which document method returns a static NodeList of ALL DOM elements matching a CSS selector?
questions.b: document.getElementsBySelectorAll()
questions.explanation: document.querySelectorAll(selector) returns all matching DOM elements in a NodeList collection.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: Which method retrieves a DOM element by its unique 'id' attribute?
questions.b: document.getElementById()
questions.explanation: document.getElementById('header') retrieves an element by its ID.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: Which method attaches an event listener handler to a DOM element in modern standards?
questions.b: element.addEventListener()
questions.explanation: element.addEventListener(type, listener, options) registers an event handler on a DOM node.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: Which method removes an event listener previously attached with addEventListener()?
questions.b: element.removeEventListener()
questions.explanation: element.removeEventListener(type, listener) unregisters the specified event listener.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What does 'event.preventDefault()' do inside an event listener callback?
questions.a: Stops event propagation up the DOM tree
questions.b: Prevents the browser's default native action for that event (such as following a link or submitting a form)
questions.explanation: event.preventDefault() suppresses the browser's default behavior for the triggered event.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What does 'event.stopPropagation()' do?
questions.b: Stops the event from bubbling up (or capturing down) the DOM hierarchy to ancestor elements
questions.explanation: event.stopPropagation() halts further propagation of the event through capturing and bubbling phases.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What are the three phases of DOM Event Flow in the W3C event model?
questions.a: Start phase, Middle phase, End phase
questions.b: Capturing Phase (trickling down), Target Phase, Bubbling Phase (bubbling up)
questions.c: Input phase, Process phase, Output phase
questions.d: Click phase, Hover phase, Release phase
questions.explanation: Events travel down from Window to Target in the Capturing phase, hit Target, and bubble back up in the Bubbling phase.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What is 'Event Delegation' in JavaScript DOM programming?
questions.a: Delegating event processing to Web Workers
questions.b: Attaching a single event listener to a common parent element to handle events for all current and future child elements via event bubbling (using event.target)
questions.explanation: Event delegation leverages bubbling by placing one listener on a parent container to manage events from all descendants.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What is the difference between 'event.target' and 'event.currentTarget'?
questions.b: 'event.target' is the actual element that triggered the event; 'event.currentTarget' is the element to which the event handler is currently attached
questions.explanation: target is the origin element clicked; currentTarget is the element currently handling the event.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: Which property on DOM elements provides convenient methods to add, remove, toggle, and check CSS classes (e.g. el.classList.add('active'))?
questions.b: element.classList
questions.explanation: element.classList provides .add(), .remove(), .toggle(), and .contains() for managing CSS classes.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: Which method creates a new DOM element node in memory (e.g. document.createElement('div'))?
questions.b: document.createElement()
questions.explanation: document.createElement(tagName) creates a new unattached HTML element node.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: Which method inserts a child DOM node as the last child of a parent element?
questions.b: parent.appendChild() or parent.append()
questions.explanation: parent.appendChild(child) inserts the child node into the DOM under the parent.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: Which method removes an element directly from the DOM in modern standards?
questions.b: element.remove()
questions.explanation: element.remove() deletes the element directly from its parent DOM tree.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What is a 'DocumentFragment' in DOM performance optimization?
questions.b: A lightweight, minimal in-memory DOM container where multiple nodes can be built before appending to the live document in a single reflow
questions.d: A temporary file stored on disk
questions.explanation: DocumentFragment batches DOM insertions in memory to prevent repeated browser reflows and repaints.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What is the difference between DOMContentLoaded and the window 'load' event?
questions.a: They fire at the exact same moment
questions.b: 'DOMContentLoaded' fires when HTML is parsed and DOM is built (without waiting for images/stylesheets); 'load' fires after the entire page and all dependent assets (images, styles) have fully loaded
questions.d: load fires before HTML is parsed
questions.explanation: DOMContentLoaded fires as soon as the DOM tree is ready; window.load waits for all external resources (images, fonts) to finish loading.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What is the 'IntersectionObserver' API used for in modern web development?
questions.b: Asynchronously observing changes in the intersection/visibility of a target element with an ancestor element or viewport (ideal for lazy-loading and infinite scroll)
questions.explanation: IntersectionObserver provides high-performance visibility detection for lazy-loading images and scroll-triggered animations.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What is the 'MutationObserver' API used for in JavaScript?
questions.b: Monitoring and reacting to DOM tree modifications (adding/removing nodes, attribute changes, text mutations)
questions.explanation: MutationObserver provides callback notifications when DOM nodes or attributes are added, removed, or changed.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What is the 'ResizeObserver' API used for?
questions.b: Reporting changes to the dimensions (content or border box size) of specific DOM elements
questions.explanation: ResizeObserver monitors element dimension changes independently of window resize events.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: Which API method schedules a function to run before the browser's next repaint to ensure smooth 60 FPS animations?
questions.b: window.requestAnimationFrame()
questions.explanation: requestAnimationFrame(callback) synchronizes animation updates with the browser's display refresh rate.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What is the 'History API' (history.pushState / history.replaceState) used for in Single-Page Applications (SPAs)?
questions.b: Modifying the browser URL and history stack without triggering a full-page reload
questions.explanation: pushState() changes the browser URL and history stack dynamically without triggering a server page reload.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What event fires on the window when the user navigates browser session history (clicking Back or Forward buttons)?
questions.b: window.onpopstate
questions.explanation: The 'popstate' event fires on active history entry changes from back/forward navigation.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: Which Web API method copies text directly into the system clipboard programmatically?
questions.b: document.copy('text')
questions.explanation: navigator.clipboard.writeText(text) asynchronously writes text to the operating system clipboard.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What is the maximum cookie size limit per cookie in standard web browsers?
questions.b: 5 Megabytes
questions.explanation: Individual HTTP cookies are limited to 4096 bytes (4KB) per cookie.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What does the 'HttpOnly' flag on a cookie do?
questions.b: Blocks client-side JavaScript (document.cookie) from accessing the cookie, protecting sensitive session tokens from XSS theft
questions.explanation: HttpOnly cookies cannot be read via JavaScript document.cookie, mitigating XSS token theft.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What does the 'SameSite' attribute on cookies (Strict / Lax / None) protect against?
questions.b: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks by restricting when cookies are sent with cross-site requests
questions.explanation: SameSite controls cross-origin cookie transmission to prevent CSRF exploits.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What is the 'Shadow DOM' in Web Components architecture?
questions.b: A self-contained, encapsulated DOM and CSS subtree scoped to a custom element, isolated from external page styles and scripts
questions.c: A backup copy of the DOM
questions.explanation: Shadow DOM encapsulates component markup and styles so they do not leak out or clash with page styles.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What does 'customElements.define('user-card', UserCard)' do in Web Components?
questions.b: Registers a new custom HTML element with the browser, connecting the tag name to an ES6 class extending HTMLElement
questions.explanation: customElements.define() registers a new autonomous custom element with the browser's DOM registry.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What is Debouncing vs Throttling in event performance optimization?
questions.b: Debouncing delays execution until a certain duration of inactivity passes (e.g. search input); Throttling guarantees execution at most once per fixed time interval (e.g. scroll listener)
questions.d: Debouncing runs on worker threads only
questions.explanation: Debounce waits for idle time before running; throttle limits execution rate to fixed intervals.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage

questions.question: What does the 'passive: true' option do in 'element.addEventListener('touchstart', fn, { passive: true })'?
questions.b: Informs the browser that the handler will never call preventDefault(), allowing the browser to optimize smooth scroll performance without waiting for JS execution
questions.c: Makes the event listener execute only once
questions.explanation: Passive event listeners guarantee no preventDefault(), enabling buttery-smooth mobile scrolling.
questions.moduleName: JS DOM, Events, Web APIs & Storage
